Asia.pdf · location 2

ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Country population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
Taiwan uses its official household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN
figure is the mainland series; Hong Kong and Macao have separate statistical series. They
are dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the
tables; where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older
internal borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current
affairs were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES

Getting to know Russia
Russia spans Europe and Asia. Moscow and Saint Petersburg are major European cities,
while Siberia and the Far East extend far beyond the Urals. A Europe volume must show the
full country without pretending that all of it lies in Europe.
Official name
Russian Federation
Capital
Moscow

17,098,246 km²

About 143,997,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.

Federal presidential republic; authoritarian
political system

annexation claims excluded
THE NATIONAL FLAG
White, blue and red form the national
tricolour. The colours have early modern
maritime associations and were restored
after Soviet rule. Popular symbolic
meanings vary and are not a single official
explanation.

[7] KOSOVO / IDENTITY
Getting to know Kosovo
Kosovo is separately administered and has declared itself an independent republic. Many
countries recognise it; Serbia and others do not. Pristina is the capital. Its profile is separate
so readers can understand the place without mistaking disputed recognition for a settled
issue.
Official name
Kosovo (Republic of Kosovo; recognition
disputed)
Capital
Pristina
Area
10,887 km²
Population
1,602,515. 2024 census; northern
municipalities include estimates because
participation was incomplete.
Languages
Albanian and Serbian
Currency
Euro (EUR), used unilaterally
Government
Parliamentary republic; separately
administered, partly recognised
Divisions
Seven districts; 38 municipalities
THE NATIONAL FLAG
A gold outline of Kosovo sits beneath six
white stars on blue. The stars are intended
to represent communities within Kosovo.
The design was adopted with the 2008
declaration of independence.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 36 36.2

[8] PORTUGAL / HISTORY
How the country took shape
Belém Tower stands beside Lisbon’s maritime gateway. It recalls imperial navigation, but that history also includes
unequal power and the movement of enslaved people.
A medieval kingdom
Portugal developed as a separate kingdom
in the twelfth century. Its border with Spain
became unusually durable, although
relations were not always peaceful.
Seafaring and empire
Maritime expansion connected Portugal
with Africa, Asia and the Americas.
Exploration also brought conquest,
exploitation and participation in the slave
trade.
Dictatorship and democratic change
The Estado Novo dictatorship lasted until
the 1974 Carnation Revolution.
Decolonisation and democratic institutions
followed. Portugal joined the European
Communities in 1986.

FRANCE / PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY
Land, water and major islands
The labels locate mountains, rivers, lakes and important islands. This
is a geographic reference map, not a relief model.
Alps
Pyrenees
Loire River
Corsica
Brittany
Coasts and mountain borders
The Atlantic and Channel face west and
north; the Mediterranean lies south. The
Alps and Pyrenees shape roads and border
crossings. The Loire, Seine, Rhône and
Garonne connect different landscapes.
Islands and overseas France
Corsica is the largest island in metropolitan
France. Grande Terre in New Caledonia is
larger among French overseas islands. The
five overseas regions include French
Guiana, giving France borders with Brazil
and Suriname.
A country beyond Europe
France also borders the Kingdom of the
Netherlands on Saint Martin. Overseas
territories have different legal
arrangements. They should not all be
counted as overseas departments or
treated as distant copies of Paris.

Europe.pdf · location 613

APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES AND SPECIAL PLACES
Places between the country chapters
Gibraltar and the British bases in Cyprus
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with a land border with Spain. Akrotiri and Dhekelia
are British Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus. They are distinct from the United Kingdom
itself and from the Republic of Cyprus.
Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
These are Crown Dependencies, not part of the United Kingdom. Jersey and Guernsey lie
near France; the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea. They govern many of their own domestic
affairs.
Faroe Islands and Greenland
Both are self-governing parts of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Faroes lie in the North
Atlantic. Greenland is geographically in North America and shares a land boundary with
Canada on Hans Island.
Åland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen
Åland is an autonomous region of Finland, with Swedish as its official language. Svalbard is
Norwegian territory governed under a special treaty framework. Jan Mayen is also
Norwegian territory, with no permanent civilian community.
References: UK Foreign Office · Government of Norway · Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Status reference date:
11 October 2026.

[2] APPENDIX B / RECOGNITION AND ADMINISTRATION
An outline cannot tell the whole story
Kosovo
Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Many states recognise it; Serbia and several other
states do not. It has a separate chapter here so its people, institutions and geography are
not lost inside a brief border note.
Cyprus
The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognised across the island apart from the British
bases. A Turkish Cypriot administration controls the north and is recognised as a state only
by Türkiye. A UN buffer zone separates parts of the island.
Georgia and Moldova
Abkhazia and South Ossetia are within Georgia’s internationally recognised borders but
beyond its government’s control. Transnistria is within Moldova’s internationally recognised
borders, with a separate de facto administration. These areas are not counted as additional
sovereign country chapters.
Ukraine and Russia
Russia’s invasion and occupation do not change Ukraine’s internationally recognised
borders in this book. Crimea and Sevastopol remain on Ukraine’s administrative map.
Russia’s chapter lists the 83 federal subjects within its internationally recognised territory.
References: United Nations · European External Action Service. These notes describe recognition and
administration, not a prediction about future settlements.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / EUROPE B.2

[3] AZERBAIJAN / HISTORY
How the country took shape
Baku’s old city reflects centuries of settlement beside the Caspian. Modern energy wealth has added a very
different skyline around its historic core.
Between larger empires
Persian, Russian and other regional powers
influenced the territory. Baku’s oil industry
grew during the imperial period. A
short-lived republic began in 1918 before
Soviet rule.
Independence and conflict
Independence returned in 1991. Wars over
Nagorno-Karabakh caused major
displacement. Azerbaijan took control of
the territory in 2023, followed by the
exodus of its Armenian population.

full country without pretending that all of it lies in Europe.

[7] RUSSIA / PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY
Land, water and major islands
The labels locate mountains, rivers, lakes and important islands. This
is a geographic reference map, not a relief model.
Ural Mountains
Volga River
Lake Baikal
Caucasus
Sakhalin
Novaya Zemlya
A country across a continent
The Urals are a common Europe–Asia
dividing line. The Volga belongs to
European Russia; Siberian rivers and Lake
Baikal belong to other vast regions. Climate
and distance vary enormously.
Major islands and far eastern ground
Sakhalin is a major Pacific island. Novaya
Zemlya and other Arctic archipelagos lie far
north. The map uses regional insets to keep
the European part readable.
Borders and annexation claims
The book shows internationally recognised
territory. Russian claims over Ukrainian
regions are excluded from the
federal-subject list. A government’s claim
and international recognition are different
things.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 45 45.12

[8] BELGIUM / HISTORY
How the country took shape
The Grand-Place reflects Brussels’s trading history and civic pride. Its guild buildings show how merchants and local
institutions helped shape a European city.
Borderlands and cities
Medieval towns grew wealthy through cloth
and trade. The region passed through
Burgundian, Habsburg and other rule
before the modern state existed.
Independence and industrialisation
Belgium became independent from the
Netherlands in 1830. Coal and
manufacturing transformed Wallonia. Later
economic growth strengthened Flanders
and shifted the country’s balance.
Empire and war
German occupation during both world wars
left painful memories. Belgian colonial rule
in Congo involved exploitation and grave
abuses. Independence abroad did not end
debate about that legacy.

UNITED KINGDOM / PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY
Land, water and major islands
The labels locate mountains, rivers, lakes and important islands. This
is a geographic reference map, not a relief model.
Great Britain
Northern Ireland
Scottish Highlands
Isle of Wight
Anglesey
Hebrides Skye
Lewis and Harris
Orkney Mainland
Shetland Mainland
Islands and coastlines
Great Britain is Europe’s largest island.
Northern Ireland occupies part of the island
of Ireland. The Hebrides, Orkney and
Shetland add northern island worlds;
Anglesey and the Isle of Wight lie farther
south.
Borders and separate jurisdictions
The UK’s main land border is with Ireland.
Crown Dependencies are not part of the UK.
Overseas Territories have their own
arrangements; Gibraltar borders Spain,
while the Sovereign Base Areas border
Cyprus.

RUSSIA / PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHY
Land, water and major islands
The labels locate mountains, rivers, lakes and important islands. This
is a geographic reference map, not a relief model.
Ural Mountains
Volga River
Lake Baikal
Caucasus
Sakhalin
Novaya Zemlya
A country across a continent
The Urals are a common Europe–Asia
dividing line. The Volga belongs to
European Russia; Siberian rivers and Lake
Baikal belong to other vast regions. Climate
and distance vary enormously.
Major islands and far eastern ground
Sakhalin is a major Pacific island. Novaya
Zemlya and other Arctic archipelagos lie far
north. The map uses regional insets to keep
the European part readable.
Borders and annexation claims
The book shows internationally recognised
territory. Russian claims over Ukrainian
regions are excluded from the
federal-subject list. A government’s claim
and international recognition are different
things.

Europe.pdf · location 614

APPENDIX B / RECOGNITION AND ADMINISTRATION
An outline cannot tell the whole story
Kosovo
Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Many states recognise it; Serbia and several other
states do not. It has a separate chapter here so its people, institutions and geography are
not lost inside a brief border note.
Cyprus
The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognised across the island apart from the British
bases. A Turkish Cypriot administration controls the north and is recognised as a state only
by Türkiye. A UN buffer zone separates parts of the island.
Georgia and Moldova
Abkhazia and South Ossetia are within Georgia’s internationally recognised borders but
beyond its government’s control. Transnistria is within Moldova’s internationally recognised
borders, with a separate de facto administration. These areas are not counted as additional
sovereign country chapters.
Ukraine and Russia
Russia’s invasion and occupation do not change Ukraine’s internationally recognised
borders in this book. Crimea and Sevastopol remain on Ukraine’s administrative map.
Russia’s chapter lists the 83 federal subjects within its internationally recognised territory.
References: United Nations · European External Action Service. These notes describe recognition and
administration, not a prediction about future settlements.

Asia.pdf · location 2

ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Country population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
Taiwan uses its official household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN
figure is the mainland series; Hong Kong and Macao have separate statistical series. They
are dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the
tables; where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older
internal borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current
affairs were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES

Africa.pdf · location 571

APPENDIX B / MAP AND RESEARCH NOTES
How this edition was made
MAPS
World and regional coasts use an open geographic dataset, with the official Indian outline
substituted consistently. Natural Earth supplies river and lake shapes. geoBoundaries
supplies administrative polygons where they match the stated framework. Major
landforms use named point locations, not a shaded-elevation model. Distant islands have
independent inset scales.
ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES
New units in Algeria, Angola, Burkina Faso, Burundi, Equatorial Guinea, Ethiopia,
Madagascar, Mali and the Republic of the Congo are included. When an available
boundary file is older than the reform, the map uses numbered locations and the note says
so. Numbering is a reading aid and does not replace official division codes.
POPULATION
The common reference is the UN World Statistics Pocketbook 2025, using mid-year
population estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. Uniform dating makes countries
easier to compare. Counts can differ from national censuses because methods, reference
dates and territorial coverage differ.
PHOTOGRAPHS AND RIGHTS
Images are sourced from Wikimedia Commons. Each country’s credit page names the file,
author and licence supplied in its metadata, with a link to the original. Some pages crop
images for layout; historic or orbital pictures are identified in captions. A reused image
does not make its photographer endorse this book.
READING FURTHER
Each country chapter ends with links for history, geography, flag background and
statistics. Recently changed frameworks have additional official sources. Political
descriptions are an October 2026 edition snapshot. This is an introductory book, not a
complete legal directory or an exhaustive history.

Serbia is centred on the Danube and the Sava, with southern hills and northern plains.
Belgrade is the capital. This book gives Kosovo a separate profile because it is separately
administered and its recognition is disputed.

Getting to know Kosovo
Kosovo is separately administered and has declared itself an independent republic. Many
countries recognise it; Serbia and others do not. Pristina is the capital. Its profile is separate
so readers can understand the place without mistaking disputed recognition for a settled
issue.
Official name
Kosovo (Republic of Kosovo; recognition
disputed)
Capital
Pristina
Area
10,887 km²
Population
1,602,515. 2024 census; northern
municipalities include estimates because
participation was incomplete.
Languages
Albanian and Serbian
Currency
Euro (EUR), used unilaterally
Government
Parliamentary republic; separately
administered, partly recognised
Divisions
Seven districts; 38 municipalities
THE NATIONAL FLAG
A gold outline of Kosovo sits beneath six
white stars on blue. The stars are intended
to represent communities within Kosovo.
The design was adopted with the 2008
declaration of independence.

Europe.pdf · location 2

EUROPE / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
Europe has more than one edge
A continent is a useful place to begin. It is not a single culture, a single
political organisation or an agreed list of borders.
What is included
The 44 sovereign countries in the UN’s European geographic grouping form the core.
Türkiye, Cyprus, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan are also included because of
their transcontinental geography or wider European connections. This makes 50 country
chapters. Kosovo receives a separate profile, with its disputed recognition explained.
What the maps do
World locators show position. Regional views name land neighbours. City maps locate
selected centres. Administrative maps and tables name the subdivisions at the level
explained in each chapter. A geographic region is not always an elected province. Distant
islands use separate insets.
What the dates mean
Most population figures are mid-2025 UN estimates, rounded to the nearest thousand.
France uses INSEE’s 1 January 2026 estimate. Vatican City uses its 31 December 2024
resident count. Kosovo uses its 2024 census results, including estimates for northern
municipalities. Government descriptions have a reference date of 11 October 2026.
Borders and disputed control
Ukraine is shown within its internationally recognised borders. Other chapters explain
disputed recognition and areas outside central government control. The maps are
geographic references, not military control maps. India’s official Survey of India outline is
used in every world locator and reproduced in the appendix.
Scope reference: UN M49 geographic grouping. Each country ends with sources and photograph credits. No printed
index is included; PDF bookmarks open the chapters.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / EUROPE F.1

Europe.pdf · location 415

KOSOVO / IDENTITY
Getting to know Kosovo
Kosovo is separately administered and has declared itself an independent republic. Many
countries recognise it; Serbia and others do not. Pristina is the capital. Its profile is separate
so readers can understand the place without mistaking disputed recognition for a settled
issue.
Official name
Kosovo (Republic of Kosovo; recognition
disputed)
Capital
Pristina
Area
10,887 km²
Population
1,602,515. 2024 census; northern
municipalities include estimates because
participation was incomplete.
Languages
Albanian and Serbian
Currency
Euro (EUR), used unilaterally
Government
Parliamentary republic; separately
administered, partly recognised
Divisions
Seven districts; 38 municipalities
THE NATIONAL FLAG
A gold outline of Kosovo sits beneath six
white stars on blue. The stars are intended
to represent communities within Kosovo.
The design was adopted with the 2008
declaration of independence.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 36 36.2

Europe.pdf · location 403

SERBIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Serbia
Serbia is centred on the Danube and the Sava, with southern hills and northern plains.
Belgrade is the capital. This book gives Kosovo a separate profile because it is separately
administered and its recognition is disputed.
Official name
Republic of Serbia
Capital
Belgrade
Area
88,499 km²
Population
About 6,689,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.
Languages
Serbian; minority languages have regional
official use.
Currency
Serbian dinar (RSD)
Government
Parliamentary republic
Divisions
Districts and Belgrade; Kosovo is profiled
separately
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Red, blue and white bands carry the
national arms on the state flag. The eagle,
shield and crown refer to historical state
symbols; the crown does not mean modern
Serbia is a monarchy.

Getting to know Russia
Russia spans Europe and Asia. Moscow and Saint Petersburg are major European cities,
while Siberia and the Far East extend far beyond the Urals. A Europe volume must show the
full country without pretending that all of it lies in Europe.

Russian Federation

Moscow

political system

tricolour. The colours have early modern
maritime associations and were restored
after Soviet rule. Popular symbolic
meanings vary and are not a single official
explanation.

[4] APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES AND SPECIAL PLACES
Places between the country chapters
Gibraltar and the British bases in Cyprus
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with a land border with Spain. Akrotiri and Dhekelia
are British Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus. They are distinct from the United Kingdom
itself and from the Republic of Cyprus.
Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
These are Crown Dependencies, not part of the United Kingdom. Jersey and Guernsey lie
near France; the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea. They govern many of their own domestic
affairs.
Faroe Islands and Greenland
Both are self-governing parts of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Faroes lie in the North
Atlantic. Greenland is geographically in North America and shares a land boundary with
Canada on Hans Island.
Åland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen
Åland is an autonomous region of Finland, with Swedish as its official language. Svalbard is
Norwegian territory governed under a special treaty framework. Jan Mayen is also
Norwegian territory, with no permanent civilian community.
References: UK Foreign Office · Government of Norway · Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Status reference date:
11 October 2026.

Europe.pdf · location 613

APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES AND SPECIAL PLACES
Places between the country chapters
Gibraltar and the British bases in Cyprus
Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory with a land border with Spain. Akrotiri and Dhekelia
are British Sovereign Base Areas on Cyprus. They are distinct from the United Kingdom
itself and from the Republic of Cyprus.
Jersey, Guernsey and the Isle of Man
These are Crown Dependencies, not part of the United Kingdom. Jersey and Guernsey lie
near France; the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea. They govern many of their own domestic
affairs.
Faroe Islands and Greenland
Both are self-governing parts of the Kingdom of Denmark. The Faroes lie in the North
Atlantic. Greenland is geographically in North America and shares a land boundary with
Canada on Hans Island.
Åland, Svalbard and Jan Mayen
Åland is an autonomous region of Finland, with Swedish as its official language. Svalbard is
Norwegian territory governed under a special treaty framework. Jan Mayen is also
Norwegian territory, with no permanent civilian community.
References: UK Foreign Office · Government of Norway · Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Status reference date:
11 October 2026.

Europe has more than one edge

Getting to know Sri Lanka
Sri Lanka is an island close to southern India. Colombo is its principal commercial centre;
parliament sits in Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte. The coast, highlands and dry northern
plains have different histories.
Official name Democratic Socialist Republic of Sri Lanka
Capital Sri Jayewardenepura Kotte (legislative); Colombo is the main executive and
commercial centre
Area 67,240 km 2
Population 23,230,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Sinhala and Tamil are official; English is a link language.
Currency Sri Lankan rupee
Government Republic with an executive president and parliament
Divisions 9 provinces
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The lion and sword are associated with the Sinhala tradition. The
orange and green stripes represent Tamil and Muslim communities.
Four bo leaves recall Buddhist virtues; the border expresses unity. The
symbols require historical context, not a single simple reading.

Q070: Are the Europe book’s maps intended to show military control in Ukraine, and what border status do they show instead?

Reference answer: No. Ukraine is shown within internationally recognised borders; the maps are geographic references, not military-control maps.

Europe.pdf · location 2
EUROPE / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
Europe has more than one edge
A continent is a useful place to begin. It is not a single culture, a single
political organisation or an agreed list of borders.
What is included
The 44 sovereign countries in the UN’s European geographic grouping form the core.
Türkiye, Cyprus, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan are also included because of
their transcontinental geography or wider European connections. This makes 50 country
chapters. Kosovo receives a separate profile, with its disputed recognition explained.
What the maps do
World locators show position. Regional views name land neighbours. City maps locate
selected centres. Administrative maps and tables name the subdivisions at the level
explained in each chapter. A geographic region is not always an elected province. Distant
islands use separate insets.
What the dates mean
Most population figures are mid-2025 UN estimates, rounded to the nearest thousand.
France uses INSEE’s 1 January 2026 estimate. Vatican City uses its 31 December 2024
resident count. Kosovo uses its 2024 census results, including estimates for northern
municipalities. Government descriptions have a reference date of 11 October 2026.
Borders and disputed control
Ukraine is shown within its internationally recognised borders. Other chapters explain
disputed recognition and areas outside central government control. The maps are
geographic references, not military control maps. India’s official Survey of India outline is
used in every world locator and reproduced in the appendix.
Scope reference: UN M49 geographic grouping. Each country ends with sources and photograph credits. No printed
index is included; PDF bookmarks open the chapters.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / EUROPE F.1

[2] APPENDIX B / RECOGNITION AND ADMINISTRATION
An outline cannot tell the whole story
Kosovo
Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Many states recognise it; Serbia and several other
states do not. It has a separate chapter here so its people, institutions and geography are
not lost inside a brief border note.
Cyprus
The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognised across the island apart from the British
bases. A Turkish Cypriot administration controls the north and is recognised as a state only
by Türkiye. A UN buffer zone separates parts of the island.
Georgia and Moldova
Abkhazia and South Ossetia are within Georgia’s internationally recognised borders but
beyond its government’s control. Transnistria is within Moldova’s internationally recognised
borders, with a separate de facto administration. These areas are not counted as additional
sovereign country chapters.
Ukraine and Russia
Russia’s invasion and occupation do not change Ukraine’s internationally recognised
borders in this book. Crimea and Sevastopol remain on Ukraine’s administrative map.
Russia’s chapter lists the 83 federal subjects within its internationally recognised territory.
References: United Nations · European External Action Service. These notes describe recognition and
administration, not a prediction about future settlements.

APPENDIX B / RECOGNITION AND ADMINISTRATION
An outline cannot tell the whole story
Kosovo
Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Many states recognise it; Serbia and several other
states do not. It has a separate chapter here so its people, institutions and geography are
not lost inside a brief border note.
Cyprus
The Republic of Cyprus is internationally recognised across the island apart from the British
bases. A Turkish Cypriot administration controls the north and is recognised as a state only
by Türkiye. A UN buffer zone separates parts of the island.
Georgia and Moldova
Abkhazia and South Ossetia are within Georgia’s internationally recognised borders but
beyond its government’s control. Transnistria is within Moldova’s internationally recognised
borders, with a separate de facto administration. These areas are not counted as additional
sovereign country chapters.
Ukraine and Russia
Russia’s invasion and occupation do not change Ukraine’s internationally recognised
borders in this book. Crimea and Sevastopol remain on Ukraine’s administrative map.
Russia’s chapter lists the 83 federal subjects within its internationally recognised territory.
References: United Nations · European External Action Service. These notes describe recognition and
administration, not a prediction about future settlements.

Europe.pdf · location 2

EUROPE / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
Europe has more than one edge
A continent is a useful place to begin. It is not a single culture, a single
political organisation or an agreed list of borders.
What is included
The 44 sovereign countries in the UN’s European geographic grouping form the core.
Türkiye, Cyprus, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan are also included because of
their transcontinental geography or wider European connections. This makes 50 country
chapters. Kosovo receives a separate profile, with its disputed recognition explained.
What the maps do
World locators show position. Regional views name land neighbours. City maps locate
selected centres. Administrative maps and tables name the subdivisions at the level
explained in each chapter. A geographic region is not always an elected province. Distant
islands use separate insets.
What the dates mean
Most population figures are mid-2025 UN estimates, rounded to the nearest thousand.
France uses INSEE’s 1 January 2026 estimate. Vatican City uses its 31 December 2024
resident count. Kosovo uses its 2024 census results, including estimates for northern
municipalities. Government descriptions have a reference date of 11 October 2026.
Borders and disputed control
Ukraine is shown within its internationally recognised borders. Other chapters explain
disputed recognition and areas outside central government control. The maps are
geographic references, not military control maps. India’s official Survey of India outline is
used in every world locator and reproduced in the appendix.
Scope reference: UN M49 geographic grouping. Each country ends with sources and photograph credits. No printed
index is included; PDF bookmarks open the chapters.

[2] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[3] NORTH AMERICA / REGIONAL OVERVIEW
The Caribbean’s 13 sovereign states
Some countries occupy one main island. Others include part of a larger
island or a chain of smaller ones.
Cuba
Haiti Dominican
Republic Jamaica
Bahamas
Barbados
Antigua and
Barbuda
Saint Kitts
and Nevis Dominica
Saint Lucia
Saint Vincent and
the Grenadines
Grenada
Trinidad and
Tobago
Shared waters, different states
Haiti and the Dominican Republic share Hispaniola. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and
Grenada divide the Grenadine island chain between them. The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic,
north of the main Antillean arc.
Countries and other places
Puerto Rico, Martinique, Guadeloupe and several other islands are not sovereign states. Their
separate constitutional arrangements appear in Appendix B. The overview highlights the 13
sovereign states in green.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA F.3

[4] APPENDIX B / NON-SOVEREIGN PLACES
North America beyond its sovereign states
These places belong in a geographic portrait of the region. Their legal
arrangements differ, so they are not counted among the 23 sovereign
countries.
Anguilla
United Kingdom · The Valley
British Overseas Territory north of Saint Martin.
Cayman Islands
United Kingdom · George Town
British Overseas Territory comprising Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman.
Montserrat
United Kingdom · Brades / Plymouth
British Overseas Territory. Plymouth is the historic capital; government operates in the north
after volcanic destruction.
Turks and Caicos Islands
United Kingdom · Cockburn Town
British Overseas Territory; Providenciales is a major population and visitor centre.
Aruba
Kingdom of the Netherlands · Oranjestad
Constituent country within the Kingdom, with its own government; not an independent
sovereign state.
Curaçao
Kingdom of the Netherlands · Willemstad
Constituent country within the Kingdom.

NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

NORTH AMERICA / REGIONAL OVERVIEW
The Caribbean’s 13 sovereign states
Some countries occupy one main island. Others include part of a larger
island or a chain of smaller ones.
Cuba
Haiti Dominican
Republic Jamaica
Bahamas
Barbados
Antigua and
Barbuda
Saint Kitts
and Nevis Dominica
Saint Lucia
Saint Vincent and
the Grenadines
Grenada
Trinidad and
Tobago
Shared waters, different states
Haiti and the Dominican Republic share Hispaniola. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines and
Grenada divide the Grenadine island chain between them. The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic,
north of the main Antillean arc.
Countries and other places
Puerto Rico, Martinique, Guadeloupe and several other islands are not sovereign states. Their
separate constitutional arrangements appear in Appendix B. The overview highlights the 13
sovereign states in green.

NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

Asia.pdf · location 2

ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Country population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
Taiwan uses its official household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN
figure is the mainland series; Hong Kong and Macao have separate statistical series. They
are dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the
tables; where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older
internal borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current
affairs were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES

Q073: Are Greenland and Puerto Rico counted among North America’s 23 sovereign countries? State how the volume classifies them.

Reference answer: No. Non-sovereign places are covered separately.

north of the main Antillean arc.
Countries and other places
Puerto Rico, Martinique, Guadeloupe and several other islands are not sovereign states. Their
separate constitutional arrangements appear in Appendix B. The overview highlights the 13
sovereign states in green.

CANADA / INTRODUCTION
Getting to know Canada
On 1 July 1867, four provinces joined to form Canada. They were not
joining an empty land. Indigenous nations had lived here for
thousands of years.
The country later stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific and into the Arctic. Distance still shapes
it. A family in Toronto, a fishing crew in Newfoundland and an Inuit household in Nunavut share a
country, but their daily lives can be very different. Canada’s story is about those differences as
much as the things that hold it together.

Capital
Ottawa
Federal official languages
English and French
Currency

Federal parliamentary democracy and
constitutional monarchy

OTTAWA IS THE CAPITAL
Toronto is Canada’s largest city, but Ottawa is the seat of the federal government. Quebec
City is the capital of Quebec; Montreal is that province’s largest city.

[4] CANADA / SOCIETY
Living in Canada
A winter coat belongs in the picture. So do rent payments, long
commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.13

[5] CANADA / REGIONAL JOURNEY
Across the country
The west coast is not the same as the Prairies. Quebec is not the
same as Atlantic Canada. A few stops reveal how much changes
along the way.
Vancouver: a Pacific port city beside mountains and
coastal waters.
Lake Louise and Mirror Lake in the Canadian Rockies.
British Columbia
Vancouver connects Canada with Pacific trade.
Coastal forests, mountains and fishing
communities share the province with drier
inland valleys. Vancouver Island contains
Victoria, the provincial capital. Indigenous
nations have long histories throughout these
lands.
The Prairies
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba contain
farmland, cities and major resource industries.
Winnipeg has deep Métis connections. Calgary
and Edmonton grew with western
development. Prairie life includes cold winters,
big skies and sharp arguments about energy
and federal policy.
Ontario
Toronto is a centre of finance and migration.
Ottawa holds federal institutions. Outside the
southern urban corridor are smaller towns,
forests and mining communities. Northern
Ontario has its own concerns about distance,
services and land.
Quebec
French language, civil law and a strong sense
of national identity shape the province.
Montreal is its largest city; Quebec City is its
capital. The St. Lawrence has long carried
trade and settlement. The province also
includes far northern communities with
different histories.
Atlantic Canada
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward
Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador look
towards the Atlantic. Fishing, ports and
migration connect them with the wider world.
Acadian communities have a distinct
French-speaking heritage. Labrador and the
island of Newfoundland differ greatly in
landscape and culture.
The three territories

[6] CANADA / GEOGRAPHY
A country on three oceans
Canada faces the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans. With about
9.98 million square kilometres of land and inland water, it is the
world’s second-largest country by total area.
Pacific
Atlantic
Arctic
UNITED STATES
GREENLAND
Baffin Island
Ottawa
Toronto
Montreal
Vancouver
Winnipeg Halifax
Iqaluit
Selected cities and neighbouring lands. Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The land neighbours
The United States borders Canada to the
south and through Alaska in the northwest. A
2022 agreement with the Kingdom of
Denmark, together with Greenland, divided
Tartupaluk/Hans Island and established
another land boundary.
Mountains, plains and rivers
The Rockies rise in the west. Mount Logan, in
Yukon’s Saint Elias Mountains, is Canada’s
highest peak. Farther east lie the Prairies and
the old rock of the Canadian Shield. The
Mackenzie river system drains towards the
Arctic; the St. Lawrence connects the Great
Lakes with the Atlantic.
Islands and fresh water
Baffin Island, in Nunavut, is Canada’s
largest island. Newfoundland and Vancouver
Island are other major islands. Lakes cover
large areas of the country. Four of the five
Great Lakes lie on the Canada-US border; Lake
Michigan is wholly in the United States.
Not one climate
Coastal British Columbia has relatively mild
winters. The Prairies face bigger seasonal
extremes. Arctic communities have long,
severe winters, while southern cities can have
hot summers. Canada is cold, but not cold in
the same way everywhere.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.5

[7] CANADA / CULTURE AND SCIENCE
Stories, music and discovery
Canadian culture comes from many languages and communities.
Some of its best-known works ask who belongs, whose history is
remembered and what the landscape means.
Books and stories
Margaret Atwood writes about power and
social control. Alice Munro found complex lives
in apparently ordinary places. Michael
Ondaatje explores memory and displacement.
Quebec’s literature has a rich French-language
tradition. Indigenous writers, including Thomas
King and Lee Maracle, challenge inherited
accounts of the country.
Music and performance
Leonard Cohen, Joni Mitchell and Céline Dion
reached listeners around the world. Inuit throat
singing and First Nations musical traditions
belong to distinct communities, not a single
generic style. Contemporary Indigenous artists
combine older practices with new forms on
their own terms.
Art and film
The Group of Seven helped make landscape
painting part of national identity. Inuit
sculpture and printmaking offer other ways of
seeing land and life. Canadian filmmaking
includes English, French and Indigenous work,
while cities such as Toronto and Vancouver
also host international productions.
Sport and public ritual
Ice hockey is the national winter sport;
lacrosse is the national summer sport. Both are
named in federal law. Lacrosse has Indigenous
origins. Fans also follow basketball, football
and other games. Local rinks and school teams
matter as much to everyday sport as
professional stars.
Science that changed lives
Research in Toronto led to insulin’s first
successful clinical use in 1922. Frederick
Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and John
Macleod all played roles. The treatment
changed diabetes care. Canada’s scientific
history also includes space robotics, medical

[8] CANADA / THE FEDERATION
Ten provinces, three territories
Each has its own government and capital. Their names matter: much
of Canadian politics turns on what should be decided locally and
what should be decided in Ottawa.
PROVINCE / TERRITORY CAPITAL YEAR*
British Columbia Victoria 1871
Alberta Edmonton 1905
Saskatchewan Regina 1905
Manitoba Winnipeg 1870
Ontario Toronto 1867
Quebec Quebec City 1867
New Brunswick Fredericton 1867
Nova Scotia Halifax 1867
Prince Edward Island Charlottetown 1873
Newfoundland and Labrador St. John’s 1949
Yukon Whitehorse 1898
Northwest Territories Yellowknife 1870
Nunavut Iqaluit 1999
*Year of joining Confederation or creation in its present named form. Boundaries have changed since; the
Northwest Territories once covered a much larger area.
WHY “PROVINCE” AND “TERRITORY” ARE DIFFERENT
Provincial powers are set out in the Constitution. Territorial powers are largely delegated by
federal law, though elected territorial governments now exercise substantial authority.
Indigenous governments add another important layer.

CANADA / INTRODUCTION
Getting to know Canada
On 1 July 1867, four provinces joined to form Canada. They were not
joining an empty land. Indigenous nations had lived here for
thousands of years.
The country later stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific and into the Arctic. Distance still shapes
it. A family in Toronto, a fishing crew in Newfoundland and an Inuit household in Nunavut share a
country, but their daily lives can be very different. Canada’s story is about those differences as
much as the things that hold it together.
Official name
Canada
Capital
Ottawa
Federal official languages
English and French
Currency
Canadian dollar (CAD)
Government
Federal parliamentary democracy and
constitutional monarchy
National day
Canada Day, 1 July
National flag
A red maple leaf between two red bands
OTTAWA IS THE CAPITAL
Toronto is Canada’s largest city, but Ottawa is the seat of the federal government. Quebec
City is the capital of Quebec; Montreal is that province’s largest city.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.2
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The maple leaf
Canada’s flag has one red maple leaf on a
white square, between two red bars. It became
the national flag in 1965. The eleven points are
a design choice; they do not represent the
provinces.
Population
41.7 million
1 July 2025 estimate, Statistics Canada.

North_America.pdf · location 17

CANADA / SOCIETY
Living in Canada
A winter coat belongs in the picture. So do rent payments, long
commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.13

North_America.pdf · location 23

CANADA / THE FEDERATION
Ten provinces, three territories
Each has its own government and capital. Their names matter: much
of Canadian politics turns on what should be decided locally and
what should be decided in Ottawa.
PROVINCE / TERRITORY CAPITAL YEAR*
British Columbia Victoria 1871
Alberta Edmonton 1905
Saskatchewan Regina 1905
Manitoba Winnipeg 1870
Ontario Toronto 1867
Quebec Quebec City 1867
New Brunswick Fredericton 1867
Nova Scotia Halifax 1867
Prince Edward Island Charlottetown 1873
Newfoundland and Labrador St. John’s 1949
Yukon Whitehorse 1898
Northwest Territories Yellowknife 1870
Nunavut Iqaluit 1999
*Year of joining Confederation or creation in its present named form. Boundaries have changed since; the
Northwest Territories once covered a much larger area.
WHY “PROVINCE” AND “TERRITORY” ARE DIFFERENT
Provincial powers are set out in the Constitution. Territorial powers are largely delegated by
federal law, though elected territorial governments now exercise substantial authority.
Indigenous governments add another important layer.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.19

North_America.pdf · location 9

CANADA / GEOGRAPHY
A country on three oceans
Canada faces the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans. With about
9.98 million square kilometres of land and inland water, it is the
world’s second-largest country by total area.
Pacific
Atlantic
Arctic
UNITED STATES
GREENLAND
Baffin Island
Ottawa
Toronto
Montreal
Vancouver
Winnipeg Halifax
Iqaluit
Selected cities and neighbouring lands. Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The land neighbours
The United States borders Canada to the
south and through Alaska in the northwest. A
2022 agreement with the Kingdom of
Denmark, together with Greenland, divided
Tartupaluk/Hans Island and established
another land boundary.
Mountains, plains and rivers
The Rockies rise in the west. Mount Logan, in
Yukon’s Saint Elias Mountains, is Canada’s
highest peak. Farther east lie the Prairies and
the old rock of the Canadian Shield. The
Mackenzie river system drains towards the
Arctic; the St. Lawrence connects the Great
Lakes with the Atlantic.
Islands and fresh water
Baffin Island, in Nunavut, is Canada’s
largest island. Newfoundland and Vancouver
Island are other major islands. Lakes cover
large areas of the country. Four of the five
Great Lakes lie on the Canada-US border; Lake
Michigan is wholly in the United States.
Not one climate
Coastal British Columbia has relatively mild
winters. The Prairies face bigger seasonal
extremes. Arctic communities have long,
severe winters, while southern cities can have
hot summers. Canada is cold, but not cold in
the same way everywhere.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.5

North_America.pdf · location 19

CANADA / REGIONAL JOURNEY
Across the country
The west coast is not the same as the Prairies. Quebec is not the
same as Atlantic Canada. A few stops reveal how much changes
along the way.
Vancouver: a Pacific port city beside mountains and
coastal waters.
Lake Louise and Mirror Lake in the Canadian Rockies.
British Columbia
Vancouver connects Canada with Pacific trade.
Coastal forests, mountains and fishing
communities share the province with drier
inland valleys. Vancouver Island contains
Victoria, the provincial capital. Indigenous
nations have long histories throughout these
lands.
The Prairies
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba contain
farmland, cities and major resource industries.
Winnipeg has deep Métis connections. Calgary
and Edmonton grew with western
development. Prairie life includes cold winters,
big skies and sharp arguments about energy
and federal policy.
Ontario
Toronto is a centre of finance and migration.
Ottawa holds federal institutions. Outside the
southern urban corridor are smaller towns,
forests and mining communities. Northern
Ontario has its own concerns about distance,
services and land.
Quebec
French language, civil law and a strong sense
of national identity shape the province.
Montreal is its largest city; Quebec City is its
capital. The St. Lawrence has long carried
trade and settlement. The province also
includes far northern communities with
different histories.
Atlantic Canada
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward
Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador look
towards the Atlantic. Fishing, ports and
migration connect them with the wider world.
Acadian communities have a distinct
French-speaking heritage. Labrador and the
island of Newfoundland differ greatly in
landscape and culture.
The three territories

[4] NIGERIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Nigeria
Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country. Abuja is the capital, Lagos a huge commercial
city, and Kano a major northern centre. Its many regions and languages make any single
portrait incomplete.
Official name Federal Republic of Nigeria
Capital Abuja
Area 923,769 km 2
Population 237,528,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages English is official; Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and hundreds of other languages are
spoken.
Currency Nigerian naira
Government Federal presidential republic
Divisions 37 states plus Federal Capital Territory
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Green, white and green form the tricolour designed by Michael Taiwo
Akinkunmi. Green represents agriculture and natural wealth; white
represents peace and unity. The flag was adopted at independence in
1960.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 23 23.2

[5] SWITZERLAND / IDENTITY
Getting to know Switzerland
Switzerland brings several language regions into one federation. Bern is the federal city,
while Zurich is the largest city. Alpine villages, industrial towns and international Geneva
have different roles. Direct votes are a routine part of politics.
Official name
Swiss Confederation
Capital
Bern (federal city)
Area
41,291 km²
Population
About 8,967,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.
Languages
German, French, Italian and Romansh
Currency
Swiss franc (CHF)
Government
Federal republic with a seven-member Federal
Council
Divisions
26 cantons
THE NATIONAL FLAG
A white cross sits on red. The square
national flag grew from older confederate
symbols. Its cross inspired the reversed
colours of the Red Cross emblem. Swiss
merchant ships use a rectangular version.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 6 6.2

[6] AUSTRIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Austria
Austria’s mountains are famous, but Vienna is a large city on the Danube. The country
stretches from Alpine valleys to eastern lowlands. Its federal states carry different histories,
accents and economic roles.
Official name
Republic of Austria
Capital
Vienna
Area
83,879 km²
Population
About 9,114,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.
Languages
German; minority languages have regional
protections.
Currency
Euro (EUR)
Government
Federal parliamentary republic
Divisions
Nine federal states
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Red, white and red come from medieval
Austrian arms. A legend connects the
bands with a crusader’s bloodstained
clothing, but it should be read as a story
rather than proven origin. State versions
add the eagle.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 8 8.2

[7] MALAYSIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Malaysia
Malaysia has two main parts separated by the South China Sea. Kuala Lumpur is the
capital; Putrajaya hosts much of the federal administration. Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo
have their own distinctive histories.
Official name Malaysia
Capital Kuala Lumpur; Putrajaya is the federal administrative centre
Area 330,803 km 2
Population 35,978,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Malay is official; English, Chinese varieties, Tamil and indigenous languages
are widely used.
Currency Malaysian ringgit
Government Federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Divisions 16 states and federal territories (13 + 3)
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Fourteen stripes and a fourteen-pointed star express the unity of the
states and federal government. Blue represents unity, yellow royal
authority, and the crescent Islamic heritage. The striped design is
known as Jalur Gemilang.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 19 19.2

[8] RUSSIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Russia
Russia extends across northern Eurasia. Moscow, its capital, lies in Europe, but most of
the land area lies in Asia. Siberian and Pacific regions therefore belong in a book about
Asia, with the country’s wider setting explained.
Official name Russian Federation
Capital Moscow
Area 17,098,246 km 2
Population 143,997,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Russian is federal official; republics may recognise additional languages.
Currency Russian ruble
Government Federal presidential republic with concentrated executive power
Divisions 83 federal subjects within internationally recognised pre-2014 territory
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The white, blue and red tricolour developed from earlier Russian flags
and was restored after Soviet rule. Popular colour interpretations
vary; there is no single binding meaning assigned to each band.

commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.

CANADA / INTRODUCTION
Getting to know Canada
On 1 July 1867, four provinces joined to form Canada. They were not
joining an empty land. Indigenous nations had lived here for
thousands of years.
The country later stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific and into the Arctic. Distance still shapes
it. A family in Toronto, a fishing crew in Newfoundland and an Inuit household in Nunavut share a
country, but their daily lives can be very different. Canada’s story is about those differences as
much as the things that hold it together.
Official name
Canada
Capital
Ottawa
Federal official languages
English and French
Currency
Canadian dollar (CAD)
Government
Federal parliamentary democracy and
constitutional monarchy
National day
Canada Day, 1 July
National flag
A red maple leaf between two red bands
OTTAWA IS THE CAPITAL
Toronto is Canada’s largest city, but Ottawa is the seat of the federal government. Quebec
City is the capital of Quebec; Montreal is that province’s largest city.

The maple leaf
Canada’s flag has one red maple leaf on a

the national flag in 1965. The eleven points are
a design choice; they do not represent the

CANADA / POLITICS
How Canada is governed
Canadians elect members of Parliament. The government must keep
the confidence of the House of Commons to remain in office.
Parliament Hill, Ottawa: the centre of federal political life.
The Crown and the government
Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The
sovereign is head of state, represented
federally by the governor general. The prime
minister leads the government. These roles
differ: the head of state is not the elected head
of government.
Parliament and elections
Parliament consists of the Crown, the elected
House of Commons and the appointed Senate.
Voters choose a local MP, rather than voting
directly for prime minister. The person able to
command Commons confidence forms a
government. A party can govern with a
majority or seek support from others.
A federal country
Ottawa handles national matters such as
defence and foreign affairs. Provinces have
major responsibilities for education, healthcare
and civil law. Territories have their own elected
governments. Indigenous governments
exercise powers through different legal and
political arrangements.
Rights and legal traditions
The Charter protects rights and freedoms,
subject to constitutional rules and limits.
Courts interpret those rules. Quebec uses civil
law for most private-law matters, while other
provinces mainly use common law. Federal law
and Indigenous legal traditions add further
layers.

The Constitution comes home
In 1982, Canada gained a domestic process for
amending its Constitution. The Charter of
Rights and Freedoms became part of it.
Quebec’s government did not consent to the
settlement, though it applies there. Nunavut’s
creation in 1999 followed a major Inuit
land-claim agreement.
A PAST THAT STILL SHAPES PUBLIC LIFE
Language rights, Indigenous land claims and provincial powers are not side issues. They grew
out of the way Canada was made, and they continue to shape what its governments can do.

Getting to know Belgium
Belgium sits between larger neighbours, yet it has its own complex federal life.
Dutch-speaking Flanders, French-speaking Wallonia and bilingual Brussels do not fit a
single language map. A small German-speaking community adds another strand.

CANADA / REGIONAL JOURNEY
Across the country
The west coast is not the same as the Prairies. Quebec is not the
same as Atlantic Canada. A few stops reveal how much changes
along the way.
Vancouver: a Pacific port city beside mountains and
coastal waters.
Lake Louise and Mirror Lake in the Canadian Rockies.
British Columbia
Vancouver connects Canada with Pacific trade.
Coastal forests, mountains and fishing
communities share the province with drier
inland valleys. Vancouver Island contains
Victoria, the provincial capital. Indigenous
nations have long histories throughout these
lands.
The Prairies
Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba contain
farmland, cities and major resource industries.
Winnipeg has deep Métis connections. Calgary
and Edmonton grew with western
development. Prairie life includes cold winters,
big skies and sharp arguments about energy
and federal policy.
Ontario
Toronto is a centre of finance and migration.
Ottawa holds federal institutions. Outside the
southern urban corridor are smaller towns,
forests and mining communities. Northern
Ontario has its own concerns about distance,
services and land.
Quebec
French language, civil law and a strong sense
of national identity shape the province.
Montreal is its largest city; Quebec City is its
capital. The St. Lawrence has long carried
trade and settlement. The province also
includes far northern communities with
different histories.
Atlantic Canada
New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward
Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador look
towards the Atlantic. Fishing, ports and
migration connect them with the wider world.
Acadian communities have a distinct
French-speaking heritage. Labrador and the
island of Newfoundland differ greatly in
landscape and culture.

North_America.pdf · location 12

CANADA / PEOPLE AND HISTORY
Before there was a Canada
The country’s history does not begin with European explorers. First
Nations and Inuit had their own homelands, trade routes, laws and
political relationships long before them.
First Nations
“First Nations” includes many distinct peoples,
not one uniform culture. Haudenosaunee,
Anishinaabe, Cree, Mi’kmaq and numerous
others have different languages and histories.
Communities exist across the country, in cities
as well as on reserves and other traditional
lands.
Inuit
Inuit homelands span the Canadian Arctic and
neighbouring regions beyond Canada. In
Canada, Inuit Nunangat includes four regions:
the Inuvialuit Settlement Region, Nunavut,
Nunavik and Nunatsiavut. Sea ice, hunting
knowledge and language remain important,
alongside modern towns, schools and
professions.
Métis
Métis peoples developed distinct communities,
cultures and political identities through their
own history, especially in the West. The Métis
Nation is not simply a label for anyone with
mixed Indigenous and European ancestry. Its
history includes the Red River community and
resistance led by Louis Riel.
Treaties and the land
Some parts of Canada are covered by historic
treaties; others involve modern agreements or
unresolved claims. Treaty partners have not
always understood promises in the same way.
Questions about land, resources and
self-government remain part of present-day
politics.
Residential schools
Governments and churches used residential
schools to separate Indigenous children from
their families and suppress their languages
and cultures. Many suffered abuse, and
thousands died. Survivors’ accounts show
damage that continued across generations.
This was not a distant episode: the system
lasted into the late twentieth century.

Q076: What currency does it use?

Reference answer: Canada uses the Canadian dollar (CAD).

[5] MALAYSIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Malaysia
Malaysia has two main parts separated by the South China Sea. Kuala Lumpur is the
capital; Putrajaya hosts much of the federal administration. Sabah and Sarawak on Borneo
have their own distinctive histories.
Official name Malaysia
Capital Kuala Lumpur; Putrajaya is the federal administrative centre
Area 330,803 km 2
Population 35,978,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Malay is official; English, Chinese varieties, Tamil and indigenous languages
are widely used.
Currency Malaysian ringgit
Government Federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Divisions 16 states and federal territories (13 + 3)
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Fourteen stripes and a fourteen-pointed star express the unity of the
states and federal government. Blue represents unity, yellow royal
authority, and the crescent Islamic heritage. The striped design is
known as Jalur Gemilang.

Getting to know Nigeria
Nigeria is Africa’s most populous country. Abuja is the capital, Lagos a huge commercial
city, and Kano a major northern centre. Its many regions and languages make any single
portrait incomplete.
Official name Federal Republic of Nigeria
Capital Abuja
Area 923,769 km 2
Population 237,528,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages English is official; Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo and hundreds of other languages are
spoken.
Currency Nigerian naira
Government Federal presidential republic
Divisions 37 states plus Federal Capital Territory
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Green, white and green form the tricolour designed by Michael Taiwo
Akinkunmi. Green represents agriculture and natural wealth; white
represents peace and unity. The flag was adopted at independence in
1960.

CANADA / SOCIETY
Living in Canada
A winter coat belongs in the picture. So do rent payments, long
commutes, neighbourhood shops and the search for a family doctor.
Toronto’s waterfront and skyline. It is Canada’s largest city, not its capital.
Languages and local identity
English and French are federal official
languages. French is especially important in
Quebec, but Francophone communities exist
elsewhere. New Brunswick is officially
bilingual. Indigenous and immigrant languages
add many more voices to Canadian life.
Migration and belonging
Immigration has changed neighbourhoods,
workplaces and family histories.
Multiculturalism is a federal policy, but
inclusion still takes work. Racism and unequal
opportunity persist. For many people, being
Canadian goes alongside close ties to another
country or community.
Healthcare and education
Provincial and territorial health plans cover
eligible residents for medically necessary
hospital and physician services. Coverage for
other care varies. Waiting times and access to
doctors can be difficult. Provinces and
territories also run education systems; there is
no single national school system.
Food, weather and weekends
Meals reflect local history and newer arrivals:
seafood in the Atlantic provinces, poutine in
Quebec, and many cuisines in big cities.
Hockey is familiar, but outdoor life also
includes skating, camping and hiking. Weather
decides what is possible, and what it costs to
get there.

CANADA / INTRODUCTION
Getting to know Canada
On 1 July 1867, four provinces joined to form Canada. They were not
joining an empty land. Indigenous nations had lived here for
thousands of years.
The country later stretched from the Atlantic to the Pacific and into the Arctic. Distance still shapes
it. A family in Toronto, a fishing crew in Newfoundland and an Inuit household in Nunavut share a
country, but their daily lives can be very different. Canada’s story is about those differences as
much as the things that hold it together.

Toronto is Canada’s largest city, but Ottawa is the seat of the federal government. Quebec
City is the capital of Quebec; Montreal is that province’s largest city.

North_America.pdf · location 15

CANADA / POLITICS
How Canada is governed
Canadians elect members of Parliament. The government must keep
the confidence of the House of Commons to remain in office.
Parliament Hill, Ottawa: the centre of federal political life.
The Crown and the government
Canada is a constitutional monarchy. The
sovereign is head of state, represented
federally by the governor general. The prime
minister leads the government. These roles
differ: the head of state is not the elected head
of government.
Parliament and elections
Parliament consists of the Crown, the elected
House of Commons and the appointed Senate.
Voters choose a local MP, rather than voting
directly for prime minister. The person able to
command Commons confidence forms a
government. A party can govern with a
majority or seek support from others.
A federal country
Ottawa handles national matters such as
defence and foreign affairs. Provinces have
major responsibilities for education, healthcare
and civil law. Territories have their own elected
governments. Indigenous governments
exercise powers through different legal and
political arrangements.
Rights and legal traditions
The Charter protects rights and freedoms,
subject to constitutional rules and limits.
Courts interpret those rules. Quebec uses civil
law for most private-law matters, while other
provinces mainly use common law. Federal law
and Indigenous legal traditions add further
layers.

have different roles. Direct votes are a routine part of politics.

CANADA / HISTORY / A FEDERATION
A country built in stages
Canada did not become independent in one dramatic break.
Provinces joined at different times, and authority shifted away from
Britain over decades.
Confederation, 1867
Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New
Brunswick formed the new Dominion on 1 July
1867. They kept provincial governments within
a federal system. The agreement addressed
colonial political and economic concerns.
Indigenous nations were not equal partners in
making it.
Expansion and resistance
Manitoba entered in 1870 after the Red River
Resistance. British Columbia joined in 1871;
Prince Edward Island followed in 1873. Railway
building helped connect the country, but
settlers’ expansion displaced Indigenous
peoples. Louis Riel was executed after the
1885 North-West Resistance.
Who could belong?
Chinese workers helped build the railway, then
faced a head tax and later exclusion. Other
communities also faced racist restrictions.
Canadians often celebrate immigration today.
That makes it especially important to
remember who was once barred, exploited or
denied equal treatment.
War and autonomy
Canada fought in the First World War and the
Second World War. Service abroad became
part of national memory, while conscription
divided the country. The Statute of
Westminster in 1931 gave Canada broad
legislative autonomy. In 1939, Canada
declared war separately from Britain.
A changing federation
Newfoundland joined in 1949; its province is
now called Newfoundland and Labrador.
Quebec’s Quiet Revolution changed
institutions and society in the 1960s.
Sovereignty referendums in 1980 and 1995
kept the future of the federation at the centre
of debate.
The Constitution comes home
In 1982, Canada gained a domestic process for
amending its Constitution.

North_America.pdf · location 21

roducts, energy,
minerals, goods and services. It also provides
development assistance and takes part in
international negotiations. Choices abroad can
reflect domestic interests as well as stated
values. Mining companies and supply chains
raise questions about responsibility beyond
national borders.
Who speaks for the country?
Foreign policy is mainly federal, but provinces,
Indigenous governments, businesses and
diaspora communities have interests of their
own. International events can therefore
become local arguments. Canada’s global role
is shaped by disagreement at home as well as
cooperation abroad.
