[5] CANADA / HISTORY / COLONIES
French and British North America
European newcomers depended on Indigenous knowledge and
partnerships. Over time, trade and settlement gave way to larger
struggles over land and power.
Old Quebec. French language and architecture remain central to the city.
Across the Atlantic
Norse visitors reached what is now
Newfoundland around the year 1000. Centuries
later, European fishing crews worked the
Atlantic coast. Jacques Cartier explored the St.
Lawrence in the 1530s. The name “Canada”
came from the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word
kanata, meaning village or settlement.
New France
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in
1608. Fur trading linked French settlers with
Indigenous trading partners, while missions
and settlement changed existing relationships.
These connections also drew communities into
conflicts between rival European powers.
Britain gains control
Britain and France fought for influence in North
America. The battle near Quebec in 1759 was a
turning point. Under the Treaty of Paris in
1763, France ceded Canada to Britain.
French-speaking communities stayed, and
their language and institutions remained part
of the country.
Other colonial histories
The story was different on the Atlantic coast
and in the West. The deportation of Acadians
began in 1755. Loyalists moved north after the
American Revolution. Fur-trading companies
expanded inland, relying on Indigenous labour
and networks while advancing commercial and
colonial claims.

Banting, Charles Best, James Collip and John
Macleod all played roles. The treatment
changed diabetes care. Canada’s scientific
history also includes space robotics, medical
research and major work in artificial
intelligence.
Symbols are only a beginning
The maple leaf, beaver and red-coated
Mountie are familiar symbols. They cannot
stand in for the whole country. A more
complete picture includes local festivals,
Indigenous language work, Quebec’s cultural
institutions and the arts created by newer
Canadians.
TWO OFFICIAL NATIONAL SPORTS
Hockey and lacrosse have legal recognition. Neither tells the whole story of what Canadians
play, watch or enjoy.

CANADA / GEOGRAPHY
A country on three oceans
Canada faces the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans. With about
9.98 million square kilometres of land and inland water, it is the
world’s second-largest country by total area.
Pacific
Atlantic
Arctic
UNITED STATES
GREENLAND
Baffin Island
Ottawa
Toronto
Montreal
Vancouver
Winnipeg Halifax
Iqaluit
Selected cities and neighbouring lands. Greenland is part of the Kingdom of Denmark.
The land neighbours
The United States borders Canada to the
south and through Alaska in the northwest. A
2022 agreement with the Kingdom of
Denmark, together with Greenland, divided
Tartupaluk/Hans Island and established
another land boundary.
Mountains, plains and rivers
The Rockies rise in the west. Mount Logan, in
Yukon’s Saint Elias Mountains, is Canada’s
highest peak. Farther east lie the Prairies and
the old rock of the Canadian Shield. The
Mackenzie river system drains towards the
Arctic; the St. Lawrence connects the Great
Lakes with the Atlantic.
Islands and fresh water
Baffin Island, in Nunavut, is Canada’s
largest island. Newfoundland and Vancouver
Island are other major islands. Lakes cover
large areas of the country. Four of the five
Great Lakes lie on the Canada-US border; Lake
Michigan is wholly in the United States.
Not one climate
Coastal British Columbia has relatively mild
winters. The Prairies face bigger seasonal
extremes. Arctic communities have long,
severe winters, while southern cities can have
hot summers. Canada is cold, but not cold in
the same way everywhere.

North_America.pdf · location 13

CANADA / HISTORY / COLONIES
French and British North America
European newcomers depended on Indigenous knowledge and
partnerships. Over time, trade and settlement gave way to larger
struggles over land and power.
Old Quebec. French language and architecture remain central to the city.
Across the Atlantic
Norse visitors reached what is now
Newfoundland around the year 1000. Centuries
later, European fishing crews worked the
Atlantic coast. Jacques Cartier explored the St.
Lawrence in the 1530s. The name “Canada”
came from the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word
kanata, meaning village or settlement.
New France
Samuel de Champlain founded Quebec in
1608. Fur trading linked French settlers with
Indigenous trading partners, while missions
and settlement changed existing relationships.
These connections also drew communities into
conflicts between rival European powers.
Britain gains control
Britain and France fought for influence in North
America. The battle near Quebec in 1759 was a
turning point. Under the Treaty of Paris in
1763, France ceded Canada to Britain.
French-speaking communities stayed, and
their language and institutions remained part
of the country.
Other colonial histories
The story was different on the Atlantic coast
and in the West. The deportation of Acadians
began in 1755. Loyalists moved north after the
American Revolution. Fur-trading companies
expanded inland, relying on Indigenous labour
and networks while advancing commercial and
colonial claims.
CHAPTER 1 / CANADA 1.9

North_America.pdf · location 22

CANADA / KEEP THE ESSENTIALS
A timeline to remember
Canada’s borders and institutions took shape over many centuries.
These dates help place the main changes in order.
Before Europeans Indigenous peoples establish societies across these lands
Around 1000 Norse settlement at L’Anse aux Meadows
1608 Champlain founds Quebec
1755 Acadian deportation begins
1763 France cedes Canada to Britain
1867 Confederation: four provinces form Canada
1870-1873 Manitoba, British Columbia and PEI join
1885 Railway completed; North-West Resistance; Riel executed
1905 Alberta and Saskatchewan become provinces
1931 Statute of Westminster advances legislative autonomy
1949 Newfoundland joins Confederation
1982 Constitution patriated; Charter becomes constitutional law
1999 Nunavut is created
2015 Truth and Reconciliation Commission issues Calls to Action
KEY TERMS
Confederation - The 1867 union and the later growth of the federation.
Federalism - Powers divided between national and provincial governments.
Confidence - The Commons support a government needs to stay in office.
Patriation - Bringing the constitutional amendment process under Canadian control.
Inuit Nunangat - The Inuit homeland in Canada, including land, water and ice.

Q078: What is the national capital of the United States, and why is it different from Washington state?

Reference answer: Washington, D.C. is the national capital; Washington state is a different place on the Pacific coast.

CHAPTER 2 / UNITED STATES 2.7

[4] USA / BEYOND THE STATES
Washington and the territories
The United States is more than fifty states. A federal district and
island territories have different political arrangements.
Washington, D.C.
The capital sits beside the Potomac River. It is
a federal district, not part of any state.
Residents elect local officials and take part in
presidential elections, but the district has no
voting senators or voting representative in the
House. Congress has special authority over it.
The five inhabited territories
Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands lie in
the Caribbean. Guam, the Northern Mariana
Islands and American Samoa lie in the
Pacific. Each has a local government. Their
constitutional position differs from that of
states.
Citizenship and representation
People born in most of these territories are US
citizens. People born in American Samoa are
generally US nationals at birth rather than
citizens, unless another rule applies. Territorial
residents do not vote for president in the
general election while residing there. Their
congressional delegates or resident
commissioner cannot vote on final House
passage.
Island names worth knowing
Puerto Rico is both a territory and its main
island; Vieques and Culebra belong to it. The
US Virgin Islands include St. Croix, St.
Thomas and St. John. The Northern Mariana
Islands include Saipan, Tinian and Rota.
Tutuila is the main population centre of
American Samoa; Guam is an island in its own
right.
Other US island possessions
The US Minor Outlying Islands include Baker,
Howland, Jarvis and Navassa islands; Johnston,
Midway and Palmyra atolls; Kingman Reef; and
Wake Island. Most have no permanent civilian
population. Some sovereignty claims are
disputed, including Navassa with Haiti and
Wake with the Marshall Islands.

[5] USA / GOVERNMENT
How the republic works
Americans elect a president separately from Congress. Power is
divided between federal institutions, states and local governments.
The US Capitol in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets.
Congress makes federal laws
The House of Representatives has 435 voting
seats, apportioned among states by
population. The Senate has two members from
each state, making 100 senators. House
members serve two-year terms; senators serve
six. Both chambers must agree on legislation
before it reaches the president.
The president and the courts
The president heads the executive branch and
serves a four-year term, subject to
constitutional limits. The Supreme Court and
lower federal courts interpret laws and hear
cases. Federal judges are nominated by the
president and confirmed by the Senate.
Different branches can check one another’s
powers.
The Electoral College
Presidential elections are decided through
electoral votes, not simply the nationwide
popular vote. States and D.C. appoint electors.
Most states award all their electoral votes to
the statewide winner; Maine and Nebraska use
different rules. This system makes the
geography of votes especially important.
States, rights and disagreement
States govern many matters involving schools,
policing, roads and elections, within federal law
and the Constitution. Tribal governments have
a distinct position. Constitutional rights are
interpreted through courts and political
disputes. Democratic and Republican parties
dominate national elections, but each contains
different views.

The capital sits beside the Potomac River. It is
a federal district, not part of any state.
Residents elect local officials and take part in
presidential elections, but the district has no
voting senators or voting representative in the
House. Congress has special authority over it.
The five inhabited territories
Puerto Rico and the US Virgin Islands lie in
the Caribbean. Guam, the Northern Mariana
Islands and American Samoa lie in the
Pacific. Each has a local government. Their
constitutional position differs from that of
states.
Citizenship and representation
People born in most of these territories are US
citizens. People born in American Samoa are
generally US nationals at birth rather than
citizens, unless another rule applies. Territorial
residents do not vote for president in the
general election while residing there. Their
congressional delegates or resident
commissioner cannot vote on final House
passage.
Island names worth knowing
Puerto Rico is both a territory and its main
island; Vieques and Culebra belong to it. The
US Virgin Islands include St. Croix, St.
Thomas and St. John. The Northern Mariana
Islands include Saipan, Tinian and Rota.
Tutuila is the main population centre of
American Samoa; Guam is an island in its own
right.
Other US island possessions
The US Minor Outlying Islands include Baker,
Howland, Jarvis and Navassa islands; Johnston,
Midway and Palmyra atolls; Kingman Reef; and
Wake Island. Most have no permanent civilian
population. Some sovereignty claims are
disputed, including Navassa with Haiti and
Wake with the Marshall Islands.

CHAPTER 2 / UNITED STATES 2.21

North_America.pdf · location 38

USA / GOVERNMENT
How the republic works
Americans elect a president separately from Congress. Power is
divided between federal institutions, states and local governments.
The US Capitol in Washington, D.C., where Congress meets.
Congress makes federal laws
The House of Representatives has 435 voting
seats, apportioned among states by
population. The Senate has two members from
each state, making 100 senators. House
members serve two-year terms; senators serve
six. Both chambers must agree on legislation
before it reaches the president.
The president and the courts
The president heads the executive branch and
serves a four-year term, subject to
constitutional limits. The Supreme Court and
lower federal courts interpret laws and hear
cases. Federal judges are nominated by the
president and confirmed by the Senate.
Different branches can check one another’s
powers.
The Electoral College
Presidential elections are decided through
electoral votes, not simply the nationwide
popular vote. States and D.C. appoint electors.
Most states award all their electoral votes to
the statewide winner; Maine and Nebraska use
different rules. This system makes the
geography of votes especially important.
States, rights and disagreement
States govern many matters involving schools,
policing, roads and elections, within federal law
and the Constitution. Tribal governments have
a distinct position. Constitutional rights are
interpreted through courts and political
disputes. Democratic and Republican parties
dominate national elections, but each contains
different views.
CHAPTER 2 / UNITED STATES 2.14

Q079: What do the fifty stars and thirteen stripes on the US flag represent?

Reference answer: Fifty states and the original thirteen colonies.

[2] PAKISTAN / IDENTITY
Getting to know Pakistan
Pakistan follows the Indus from northern mountains to the Arabian Sea. Islamabad is the
capital, Karachi the largest commercial centre, and Lahore a historic cultural hub. These
cities tell quite different stories.
Official name Islamic Republic of Pakistan
Capital Islamabad
Area 881,913 km 2
Population 255,220,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Urdu and English; Punjabi, Pashto, Sindhi, Balochi and many other
languages are spoken.
Currency Pakistani rupee
Government Federal parliamentary republic
Divisions 7 provinces / territory / separately administered areas
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The green field and crescent express Islamic heritage. The white
stripe represents religious minorities; the white crescent and star are
associated with progress and knowledge. The design was adopted at
independence in 1947.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 2 2.2

[3] CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC / IDENTITY
Getting to know Central African Republic
The Central African Republic lies inland, between the Sahel and the Congo Basin. Bangui
stands beside the Ubangi River. Long distances and limited roads make transport a daily
concern.
Official name Central African Republic
Capital Bangui
Area 622,984 km 2
Population 5,513,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Sango and French
Currency Central African CFA franc (XAF)
Government Presidential republic
Divisions 20 prefectures including Bangui
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Four horizontal bands combine blue, white, green and yellow, crossed
by a red vertical stripe. The design brings together colours associated
with France and Africa. Red expresses a shared human bond; the star
represents hope.

Official name Malaysia
Capital Kuala Lumpur; Putrajaya is the federal administrative centre
Area 330,803 km 2

THE NATIONAL FLAG
Fourteen stripes and a fourteen-pointed star express the unity of the
states and federal government. Blue represents unity, yellow royal
authority, and the crescent Islamic heritage. The striped design is
known as Jalur Gemilang.

Capital Lomé

Population 5,731,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages English is official; many indigenous languages are spoken.
Currency Liberian dollar; U.S. dollars also circulate
Government Presidential republic
Divisions 15 counties
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Red and white stripes and a blue canton recall the United States,
reflecting the state’s founding links. Eleven stripes commemorate
signatories of the declaration of independence; the lone star
symbolised the independent African republic.

AUSTRALIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Australia
Australia is a continent-sized country with most of its people living near the coast. Sydney
is the largest familiar gateway. Canberra is the capital. The country’s first peoples have
histories far older than the state founded in 1901.
Official name Commonwealth of Australia
Capital Canberra
Population 26,974,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 7,688,287 km²
Languages English is the main public language; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
languages and many migrant languages are spoken.
Currency Australian dollar
Government Federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Directory level 8 states and main territories (6 + 2)
THE FLAG
The Union Jack recalls British connections. The seven-point
Commonwealth Star represents the states and territories. The Southern
Cross places the country in the southern sky. Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander flags have their own recognised status.

Africa.pdf · location 567

WESTERN SAHARA / FLAGS AND CLAIMS
Two flags, two political positions
The flags identify the authorities and claims described in this section. They do not decide
sovereignty.
MOROCCO
The red field and green star are the Moroccan
national flag. Morocco uses it in the parts of
Western Sahara it administers. Its meaning and
history are explained in the Morocco chapter.
SAHRAWI ARAB DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC
Black, white and green bands, a red triangle, and a
red crescent and star identify the Sahrawi
independence movement and the republic it
proclaimed. Its recognition and territorial control
differ from its claim to the whole territory.
READING THE DISTINCTION
A national flag can be a symbol of identity, a record of a liberation movement and a
statement of a territorial claim. Here those roles overlap. Morocco administers most of the
territory; the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic belongs to the African Union. The UN
continues to list Western Sahara separately as a Non-Self-Governing Territory.
Flag artwork: Wikimedia Commons. The linked file records the source and licence.

SOMALIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Somalia
Somalia has a long Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden coastline. Mogadishu is the federal
capital. Political authority is divided, and the map needs to explain that complexity rather
than conceal it.
Official name Federal Republic of Somalia
Capital Mogadishu
Area 637,657 km 2
Population 19,655,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Somali and Arabic are official.
Currency Somali shilling; U.S. dollars are widely used
Government Federal parliamentary republic with fragmented territorial authority
Divisions 18 traditional geographic regions
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The pale blue field carries a white five-pointed star. Its points
traditionally represent Somali-inhabited regions across several
territories; this symbolism is not a statement that those areas belong
to today’s Somali state.

[3] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[4] MEXICO / THE WIDER WORLD
Mexico beyond its borders
Mexico belongs to North America geographically and has deep
connections across Latin America and the wider world.
The United States and Canada
Trade links factories, farms and consumers
across the three countries. Family ties across
the US border are equally important. Migration,
security and trade policy can create tension
even when cooperation is extensive. Mexico is
a partner with interests of its own, not simply
an extension of its northern neighbour.
Southern neighbours
Guatemala and Belize share land borders with
Mexico. Trade, river systems and community
ties cross them. Mexico is also a destination
and transit country for migrants from farther
south. Their experiences bring questions of
work, safety, asylum and public services into
local life.
Diplomacy and sovereignty
Non-intervention and national sovereignty
have been influential principles in Mexican
diplomacy. Mexico participates in the United
Nations, the G20 and regional organisations.
Its responses to particular conflicts and
governments change with circumstances.
Diplomatic principles do not remove
disagreement at home.
Culture and the diaspora
Mexican communities abroad maintain family,
cultural and economic ties. Food, film,
literature and music cross borders with them.
Mexican Americans have their own histories
within the United States. National identity can
be lived through more than one language or
place.
Mexico and India
The two countries have diplomatic, commercial
and cultural connections. Both take part in
international forums and have large, diverse
societies. Trade, education and business
create areas of exchange. Their relationship is
one part of Mexico’s wider effort to maintain
links beyond North America.
Shared problems need cooperation

[7] APPENDIX B / NON-SOVEREIGN PLACES
North America beyond its sovereign states
These places belong in a geographic portrait of the region. Their legal
arrangements differ, so they are not counted among the 23 sovereign
countries.
Anguilla
United Kingdom · The Valley
British Overseas Territory north of Saint Martin.
Cayman Islands
United Kingdom · George Town
British Overseas Territory comprising Grand Cayman, Cayman Brac and Little Cayman.
Montserrat
United Kingdom · Brades / Plymouth
British Overseas Territory. Plymouth is the historic capital; government operates in the north
after volcanic destruction.
Turks and Caicos Islands
United Kingdom · Cockburn Town
British Overseas Territory; Providenciales is a major population and visitor centre.
Aruba
Kingdom of the Netherlands · Oranjestad
Constituent country within the Kingdom, with its own government; not an independent
sovereign state.
Curaçao
Kingdom of the Netherlands · Willemstad
Constituent country within the Kingdom.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / NORTH AMERICA B.2

[8] HONDURAS / IDENTITY
Getting to know Honduras
Honduras has two coasts, but most of its land is mountainous. A coffee-growing town in the
west feels different from a Caribbean port or a community in La Mosquitia. Tegucigalpa
shares the capital district with Comayagüela. San Pedro Sula is a major centre of industry
and trade.
Official name
Republic of Honduras
Capital
Tegucigalpa
Area
112,492 square kilometres
Population
About 11,000,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.
Languages
Spanish; Garifuna, Indigenous and island
languages also matter.
Currency
Lempira (HNL)
Government
Presidential republic
Administrative divisions
18 departments
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Five stars sit between blue bands. They
recall the five states of the former Central
American federation: Guatemala, El
Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa
Rica. The blue bands evoke the seas on
either side of Central America. The white
band is associated with peace.
Population figures refer to a named year and are
rounded. They are estimates, not a count of people
made on this chapter’s publication date.

[8] BEYOND THE FOURTEEN CHAPTERS
Different places, different status
SELF-GOVERNING STATES IN FREE ASSOCIATION
The Cook Islands and Niue have their own governments and international treaty-making
capacity. Their free association with New Zealand includes constitutional responsibilities
and citizenship links. They are not counted among the fourteen UN-member country
chapters, and should not be described as ordinary New Zealand provinces.
INDEPENDENT COMPACT STATES
Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands are independent
countries. Their Compacts of Free Association with the United States are different from
the relationship of a U.S. territory such as Guam. A compact covers agreed responsibilities
and assistance; it does not erase sovereignty.
TERRITORIES AND PARTS OF LARGER STATES
Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Tokelau, New Caledonia, French
Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn and Norfolk Island have different arrangements.
Hawaiʻi is a U.S. state. Rapa Nui is part of Chile. Both belong in a geographic discussion of
the Pacific without becoming extra independent countries.
GEOGRAPHY AND COUNTING
A continent’s boundary is a convention. Indonesia’s western New Guinea and Chile’s Rapa
Nui help show why geographic, statistical and political groupings differ. Bougainville
remains within Papua New Guinea while its post-referendum constitutional process
continues. New Caledonia’s future arrangements are debated; this book identifies its
present French connection rather than declaring an implemented new state.

Asia.pdf · location 2

ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Country population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
Taiwan uses its official household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN
figure is the mainland series; Hong Kong and Macao have separate statistical series. They
are dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the
tables; where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older
internal borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current
affairs were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES

Niue
Capital: Alofi
The yellow field and stars within the Union Jack make Niue’s flag distinctive.

N
Alofi
Niue Island
Niue entered self-government in free association with New Zealand in 1974. It is a single
raised-coral island rather than a chain of low atolls. Alofi is the main government centre.
Niuean and English are used, and the New Zealand dollar is the currency. An elected
assembly and premier form the government. Many people of Niuean descent live overseas,
especially in New Zealand. Families and local institutions therefore have close links across
the ocean. Tourism, public services and assistance are important, while cyclones, water and
transport costs affect island life. Free association preserves a distinct local government and
international capacity.

[7] PACIFIC TERRITORIES / DIRECTORY
United States and New Zealand
GUAM
U.S. territory; main government centre Hagåtña. The island is home to Chamorro heritage
and major military installations. It is different from an independent compact state.
NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS
A commonwealth in political union with the United States; Saipan is the main government
centre. The islands include Saipan, Tinian, Rota and northern volcanic islands.
AMERICAN SAMOA
U.S. territory centred on Tutuila and the Pago Pago harbour area, with government
institutions at Fagatogo and Utulei. The Manuʻa group and other islands broaden the map.
It is separate from independent Samoa.
TOKELAU
New Zealand territory consisting of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo. Decisions involve
island institutions and a national General Fono. There is no single conventional capital
city.
HAWAIʻI
A U.S. state, not a dependent territory or separate country. Honolulu is the capital.
Hawaiian language and culture, the overthrow of the kingdom and annexation belong
within its history.
U.S. MINOR OUTLYING ISLANDS
Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Johnston, Kingman Reef, Midway, Palmyra and Wake have
different administrative and environmental roles. They are not added as independent
countries.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER T T.5

[8] NAURU / HISTORY
How the present took shape
EARLIER LIVES AND TURNING POINTS
Nauruan communities lived on the island before German annexation in 1888. Phosphate
discovery brought intensive extraction and foreign control. Australia, New Zealand and
Britain administered the island after the First World War. Japanese occupation during the
Second World War included deportation and suffering. Independence came in 1968.
GOVERNMENT, WORK AND PUBLIC LIFE
Parliament elects a president who serves as both head of state and head of government.
Fourteen districts are listed, but they do not have fourteen separate provincial capitals.
Phosphate income once supported considerable wealth; depletion and financial problems
changed that position. Fishing revenues, services and arrangements connected with
Australia have shaped recent finances. Offshore migration processing has also drawn
major human-rights scrutiny.
This 2007 photograph records phosphate mining and its effects on the land. Resource extraction brought
income but also left a lasting environmental burden.
Image: Lorrie Graham/AusAID · CC BY 2.0 · Full image record ↗

Ocenia.pdf · location 154

PACIFIC TERRITORIES / DIRECTORY
United States and New Zealand
GUAM
U.S. territory; main government centre Hagåtña. The island is home to Chamorro heritage
and major military installations. It is different from an independent compact state.
NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS
A commonwealth in political union with the United States; Saipan is the main government
centre. The islands include Saipan, Tinian, Rota and northern volcanic islands.
AMERICAN SAMOA
U.S. territory centred on Tutuila and the Pago Pago harbour area, with government
institutions at Fagatogo and Utulei. The Manuʻa group and other islands broaden the map.
It is separate from independent Samoa.
TOKELAU
New Zealand territory consisting of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo. Decisions involve
island institutions and a national General Fono. There is no single conventional capital
city.
HAWAIʻI
A U.S. state, not a dependent territory or separate country. Honolulu is the capital.
Hawaiian language and culture, the overthrow of the kingdom and annexation belong
within its history.
U.S. MINOR OUTLYING ISLANDS
Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Johnston, Kingman Reef, Midway, Palmyra and Wake have
different administrative and environmental roles. They are not added as independent
countries.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER T T.5

Ocenia.pdf · location 116

NAURU / HISTORY
How the present took shape
EARLIER LIVES AND TURNING POINTS
Nauruan communities lived on the island before German annexation in 1888. Phosphate
discovery brought intensive extraction and foreign control. Australia, New Zealand and
Britain administered the island after the First World War. Japanese occupation during the
Second World War included deportation and suffering. Independence came in 1968.
GOVERNMENT, WORK AND PUBLIC LIFE
Parliament elects a president who serves as both head of state and head of government.
Fourteen districts are listed, but they do not have fourteen separate provincial capitals.
Phosphate income once supported considerable wealth; depletion and financial problems
changed that position. Fishing revenues, services and arrangements connected with
Australia have shaped recent finances. Offshore migration processing has also drawn
major human-rights scrutiny.
This 2007 photograph records phosphate mining and its effects on the land. Resource extraction brought
income but also left a lasting environmental burden.
Image: Lorrie Graham/AusAID · CC BY 2.0 · Full image record ↗

[4] FIJI / CULTURE
Life beyond the headline
Village gatherings, church life and yaqona / kava ceremonies are important in many
iTaukei communities. Indo-Fijian food, language, festivals and religious traditions add
another major strand. Rugby is a widely shared enthusiasm. Respecting local
protocols matters more than copying a gesture from a holiday photograph.
Traditional buildings at Navala show village architecture on Viti Levu. Housing belongs within family, land and
community relationships, not simply a picturesque scene.

Ocenia.pdf · location 2
OCEANIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A region connected by ocean
THE COUNTRIES
This volume has fourteen chapters for Oceania’s UN-member countries. Australia and
New Zealand lead, followed by the independent Pacific island states. The Cook Islands and
Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand, not ordinary
dependent territories; a separate section explains them. Other territories and Pacific
places are identified with their constitutional links.
PICTURES THAT BELONG TO THE STORY
Every country has three different images: its opener, a history illustration and a culture or
daily-life image. Historic documents and photographs are identified in captions. Images
are not generated scenes. Photographer and licence credits link to the original records.
The pictures are not reused between chapters.
DATES AND ADMINISTRATIVE LEVELS
Population uses UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand, except Samoa’s
official November 2021 census. These dates are printed beside the figures. Directories
state their level: provinces, states, districts, councils or, for Kiribati, statistical districts. A
reference centre is not automatically a separate capital.
READING AN ISLAND MAP
The Pacific-centred views carry longitudes eastward beyond 180 degrees. This joins
islands that ordinary world maps split at the edge. It does not change their locations or
political status. Small islands have point markers and insets; dots are deliberately larger
than the land so the reader can find them. Insets have different scales. Sea neighbours are
selected nearby countries, not claims about maritime borders.
PAGE NUMBERS AND MAP CONVENTIONS
Country pages use 1.1, 1.2 and so on. PDF bookmarks open complete chapters; there is no
printed index.

The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic, southeast of Florida and north of Cuba. Hundreds of

[2] APPENDIX B / UNDERSTANDING THE MAPS
Dates, distances and careful reading
POPULATION DATES
Thirteen country figures are UN World Statistics Pocketbook 2025 mid-year estimates
rounded to the nearest thousand. Samoa uses its official November 2021 census count
because the matching UN country page was unavailable during production. The census
date is explicit; it is not relabelled as a 2025 estimate.
DIRECTORIES
Every directory declares its level. Australia includes the six states and two main
self-governing territories. New Zealand adds Chatham Islands outside the sixteen regions.
Fiji uses divisions plus Rotuma. Kiribati uses five statistical districts. Tuvalu’s eight
council areas administer nine islands. Nauru’s districts have no separate provincial
capitals. These distinctions prevent a neat-looking table from becoming a misleading one.
COORDINATES AND OUTLINES
Natural Earth supplies coasts, rivers and lakes. Approximate settlement and island
coordinates support the labels. Locator points replace precise division borders where
these are not supplied. Dots enlarge small islands so they remain visible; the marker size
is not the land area. Geographic maps are not nautical charts.
THE 180-DEGREE MERIDIAN AND THE DATE LINE
A longitude beyond 180° east is another way to plot a place normally written with west
longitude. The maps join the Pacific across the usual page edge. The International Date
Line bends around political choices and does not follow the 180-degree meridian
everywhere. A geographic wrap must not be mistaken for a complete map of time zones.

[3] TUNISIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Tunisia
Tunisia is small beside Algeria and Libya, but its coast has a long Mediterranean history.
Tunis is the political centre. Sfax, Sousse, inland towns and southern oases tell other parts
of the story.
Official name Republic of Tunisia
Capital Tunis
Area 163,610 km 2
Population 12,349,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Arabic; Tunisian Arabic is spoken daily and French is widely used.
Currency Tunisian dinar
Government Presidential republic
Divisions 24 governorates
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The red field and white disc carry a red crescent and star. The design
dates to the nineteenth-century Tunisian monarchy. It retained its
place after the republic replaced the monarchy in 1957.

Getting to know Samoa

Capital Apia

Languages Samoan and English
Currency Samoan tālā

the national design.

Getting to know Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
The country combines Saint Vincent with the northern part of the Grenadines. Kingstown

Capital
Kingstown
Area
389 square kilometres

Parliamentary constitutional monarchy

Six parishes
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Blue, gold and green vertical bands
surround three green diamonds in a V. Blue
evokes sea and sky; gold the sunshine and
sands; green the land. The diamonds recall
Saint Vincent’s name and its place among

[7] SUDAN / IDENTITY
Getting to know Sudan
Sudan’s history joins the Nile valley, Red Sea coast, Darfur and the wider Sahel. Khartoum
grew where the Blue and White Nile meet. The war that began in 2023 has disrupted
cities and communities across the country.
Official name Republic of the Sudan
Capital Khartoum; Port Sudan has hosted wartime government offices
Area 1,886,068 km 2
Population 51,662,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Arabic and English
Currency Sudanese pound
Government Republic fractured by civil war
Divisions 18 states
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Red, white, black and green place the flag within the pan-Arab
tradition. The current design dates to 1970. Its colours carry national
and political associations; older independent Sudan used a different
tricolour.

[8] PANAMA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Panama
Panama links Central America to South America. Its canal also links Atlantic and Pacific
shipping routes. The capital’s skyline can make the country look like a single modern
service hub. Travel away from it and the picture changes: farming towns, islands, forest
communities and Indigenous territories fill the map.
Official name
Republic of Panama
Capital
Panama City
Area
75,417 square kilometres
Population
About 4,600,000; mid-2025 UN estimate.
Languages
Spanish; Indigenous and Afro-Caribbean
languages are also used.
Currency
Balboa (PAB) and United States dollar
(USD)
Government
Presidential republic
Administrative divisions
Ten provinces and six Indigenous
comarcas, with different administrative
levels
THE NATIONAL FLAG
Four quarters hold red and blue blocks and
two stars on white. The colours originally
referred to rival political traditions; white
expresses peace between them. The stars
are associated with civic ideals. The design
belongs to the republic founded in 1903.

Asia.pdf · location 540

APPENDIX C / RESEARCH AND MAP NOTES
How to use the dates and directories
POPULATION
The common country reference is the UN World Statistics Pocketbook 2025: mid-year
estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. Taiwan uses the Ministry of the Interior’s
household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN mainland series is
separate from Hong Kong and Macao. These figures have different coverage from a count
of every person associated with a national identity.
ADMINISTRATIVE CHANGES
The directories include recent reforms in Vietnam, Indonesia, Iraq, Kazakhstan and
elsewhere. Where a boundary file is older than the named framework, numbered locator
points replace its internal borders. Capitals may be shared, seasonal or outside the unit
they serve. A reference centre is not presented as an independent provincial capital.
MAPS
Natural Earth supplies coasts, lakes and rivers. geoBoundaries supplies administrative
geometry where it matches the stated level. The official Survey of India outline is
substituted consistently, and conflicting overlapping country shapes are trimmed around
it. Named points identify major landforms; the physical maps are not elevation-shaded
surveys. Small and remote islands use separate insets.
PHOTOGRAPHS AND CREDITS
Opening images and repeated details are sourced from Wikimedia Commons. Each
chapter names the exact file and links to its author and licence record; available metadata
is printed in the credit. Some images are cropped for layout. Historic, orbital or composite
images are identified where used. Rights and full-resolution originals should be checked at
the linked file before further publication.
SCOPE
This is an introductory country book, not an exhaustive legal directory or a live news
service.

Getting to know Bahamas
The Bahamas lies in the Atlantic, southeast of Florida and north of Cuba. Hundreds of
islands and many more small cays stretch across shallow banks. Nassau is on New
Providence. Calling the country a single Caribbean island misses both its Atlantic location
and the distances between its communities.

TUNISIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Tunisia
Tunisia is small beside Algeria and Libya, but its coast has a long Mediterranean history.
Tunis is the political centre. Sfax, Sousse, inland towns and southern oases tell other parts
of the story.
Official name Republic of Tunisia
Capital Tunis
Area 163,610 km 2
Population 12,349,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate; rounded to the nearest thousand.
Languages Arabic; Tunisian Arabic is spoken daily and French is widely used.
Currency Tunisian dinar
Government Presidential republic
Divisions 24 governorates
THE NATIONAL FLAG
The red field and white disc carry a red crescent and star. The design
dates to the nineteenth-century Tunisian monarchy. It retained its
place after the republic replaced the monarchy in 1957.

SAINT VINCENT AND THE GRENADINES / IDENTITY
Getting to know Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
The country combines Saint Vincent with the northern part of the Grenadines. Kingstown
lies on Saint Vincent, the largest island. Bequia, Mustique, Canouan, Mayreau and Union
Island have distinct local lives farther south. The Grenadine chain continues into Grenada,
so an island-chain name is not the same as a national boundary.

Q086: Why do the Oceania maps carry longitudes eastward beyond 180 degrees, and does this change island locations or political status?

Reference answer: To keep Pacific islands together rather than splitting them at the map edge; their locations and political status do not change.

POPULATION DATES

because the matching UN country page was unavailable during production. The census
date is explicit; it is not relabelled as a 2025 estimate.
DIRECTORIES
Every directory declares its level. Australia includes the six states and two main
self-governing territories. New Zealand adds Chatham Islands outside the sixteen regions.
Fiji uses divisions plus Rotuma. Kiribati uses five statistical districts. Tuvalu’s eight
council areas administer nine islands. Nauru’s districts have no separate provincial
capitals. These distinctions prevent a neat-looking table from becoming a misleading one.
COORDINATES AND OUTLINES
Natural Earth supplies coasts, rivers and lakes. Approximate settlement and island
coordinates support the labels. Locator points replace precise division borders where
these are not supplied. Dots enlarge small islands so they remain visible; the marker size
is not the land area. Geographic maps are not nautical charts.
THE 180-DEGREE MERIDIAN AND THE DATE LINE
A longitude beyond 180° east is another way to plot a place normally written with west
longitude. The maps join the Pacific across the usual page edge. The International Date
Line bends around political choices and does not follow the 180-degree meridian
everywhere. A geographic wrap must not be mistaken for a complete map of time zones.

[5] BEYOND THE FOURTEEN CHAPTERS
Different places, different status
SELF-GOVERNING STATES IN FREE ASSOCIATION
The Cook Islands and Niue have their own governments and international treaty-making
capacity. Their free association with New Zealand includes constitutional responsibilities
and citizenship links. They are not counted among the fourteen UN-member country
chapters, and should not be described as ordinary New Zealand provinces.
INDEPENDENT COMPACT STATES
Palau, the Federated States of Micronesia and the Marshall Islands are independent
countries. Their Compacts of Free Association with the United States are different from
the relationship of a U.S. territory such as Guam. A compact covers agreed responsibilities
and assistance; it does not erase sovereignty.
TERRITORIES AND PARTS OF LARGER STATES
Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, Tokelau, New Caledonia, French
Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna, Pitcairn and Norfolk Island have different arrangements.
Hawaiʻi is a U.S. state. Rapa Nui is part of Chile. Both belong in a geographic discussion of
the Pacific without becoming extra independent countries.
GEOGRAPHY AND COUNTING
A continent’s boundary is a convention. Indonesia’s western New Guinea and Chile’s Rapa
Nui help show why geographic, statistical and political groupings differ. Bougainville
remains within Papua New Guinea while its post-referendum constitutional process
continues. New Caledonia’s future arrangements are debated; this book identifies its
present French connection rather than declaring an implemented new state.
READING FURTHER

foreign ministry explains free association. The Pacific Islands Forum brings together

OCEANIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A region connected by ocean
THE COUNTRIES
This volume has fourteen chapters for Oceania’s UN-member countries. Australia and
New Zealand lead, followed by the independent Pacific island states. The Cook Islands and
Niue are self-governing states in free association with New Zealand, not ordinary
dependent territories; a separate section explains them. Other territories and Pacific
places are identified with their constitutional links.
PICTURES THAT BELONG TO THE STORY
Every country has three different images: its opener, a history illustration and a culture or
daily-life image. Historic documents and photographs are identified in captions. Images
are not generated scenes. Photographer and licence credits link to the original records.
The pictures are not reused between chapters.
DATES AND ADMINISTRATIVE LEVELS
Population uses UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand, except Samoa’s
official November 2021 census. These dates are printed beside the figures. Directories
state their level: provinces, states, districts, councils or, for Kiribati, statistical districts. A
reference centre is not automatically a separate capital.
READING AN ISLAND MAP
The Pacific-centred views carry longitudes eastward beyond 180 degrees. This joins
islands that ordinary world maps split at the edge. It does not change their locations or
political status. Small islands have point markers and insets; dots are deliberately larger
than the land so the reader can find them. Insets have different scales. Sea neighbours are
selected nearby countries, not claims about maritime borders.
PAGE NUMBERS AND MAP CONVENTIONS
Country pages use 1.1, 1.2 and so on. PDF bookmarks open complete chapters; there is no
printed index.

[3] SOLOMON ISLANDS / IDENTITY
Getting to know Solomon Islands
Solomon Islands is an archipelago east of Papua New Guinea. Honiara stands on
Guadalcanal. The country includes large forested islands and small outer islands spread
over a wide area. Languages and local identities vary from one island to the next.
Official name Solomon Islands
Capital Honiara
Population 839,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 28,896 km²
Languages English is official; Solomon Islands Pijin is widely used alongside many local
languages.
Currency Solomon Islands dollar
Government Parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Directory level 10 provinces and capital administration (9 + 1)
THE FLAG
Blue represents the sea, green the land and yellow sunshine. The five
white stars originally reflected an earlier five-district framework. They are
not a count of today’s provinces.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 5 5.2

[4] TUVALU / IDENTITY
Getting to know Tuvalu
Tuvalu is a small country of nine low islands in the Pacific. Its land area is tiny compared
with the ocean around it. Funafuti is the capital atoll, with government offices on
Fongafale. “Small” does not mean that its voice or identity is unimportant.
Official name Tuvalu
Capital Funafuti; government offices are on Fongafale islet
Population 10,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 26.26 km²
Languages Tuvaluan and English
Currency Australian dollar; Tuvalu also issues local coins
Government Parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Directory level 8 island council areas
THE FLAG
The Union Jack recalls British connections. Nine yellow stars represent
the nine islands. Their arrangement roughly echoes island geography
rather than forming an astronomical constellation.

AUSTRALIA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Australia
Australia is a continent-sized country with most of its people living near the coast. Sydney
is the largest familiar gateway. Canberra is the capital. The country’s first peoples have
histories far older than the state founded in 1901.
Official name Commonwealth of Australia
Capital Canberra
Population 26,974,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 7,688,287 km²
Languages English is the main public language; Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander
languages and many migrant languages are spoken.
Currency Australian dollar
Government Federal parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Directory level 8 states and main territories (6 + 2)
THE FLAG
The Union Jack recalls British connections. The seven-point
Commonwealth Star represents the states and territories. The Southern
Cross places the country in the southern sky. Aboriginal and Torres Strait
Islander flags have their own recognised status.

[5] SAMOA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Samoa
Samoa is centred on Savaiʻi and Upolu. Apia is the capital, on Upolu’s north coast. The
country is independent and distinct from American Samoa, which lies to the east and has a
different political status.
Official name Independent State of Samoa
Capital Apia
Population 205,557 — Samoa official census, November 2021; not a 2025 estimate.
Area 2,831 km²
Languages Samoan and English
Currency Samoan tālā
Government Parliamentary republic with a head of state chosen under constitutional
arrangements
Directory level 11 traditional political districts
THE FLAG
Five white stars form the Southern Cross on a blue panel. Red, white and
blue are associated with courage, purity and freedom in explanations of
the national design.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 7 7.2

[6] NEW ZEALAND / IDENTITY
Getting to know New Zealand
New Zealand sits across the Tasman Sea from Australia. It is often called Aotearoa. Its two
main islands carry very different landscapes, while smaller and distant islands widen the
map. Wellington is the capital; Auckland is the largest city.
Official name New Zealand / Aotearoa
Capital Wellington
Population 5,252,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 263,310 km²
Languages English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are official; English received
explicit statutory recognition in 2026.
Currency New Zealand dollar
Government Parliamentary constitutional monarchy
Directory level 17 regions and Chatham Islands (16 + 1)
THE FLAG
The Union Jack records British ties. Four red stars edged in white
represent the Southern Cross. They differ from the stars on Australia’s
flag, so the two should not be treated as interchangeable.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / CHAPTER 2 2.2

[7] VANUATU / IDENTITY
Getting to know Vanuatu
Vanuatu is a chain of islands between Fiji and Australia. Port Vila is the capital, on Efate.
Luganville on Espiritu Santo is another important town. Many communities speak a local
language as well as Bislama.
Official name Republic of Vanuatu
Capital Port Vila
Population 335,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 12,189 km²
Languages Bislama, English and French are official; many indigenous languages are
spoken.
Currency Vanuatu vatu
Government Parliamentary republic
Directory level 6 provinces
THE FLAG
The Y shape echoes the island chain. Red, green and black have national
symbolic meanings, while yellow is associated with Christian faith. The
boar’s tusk and crossed namele leaves refer to wealth, customary life
and peace.

SAMOA / IDENTITY
Getting to know Samoa
Samoa is centred on Savaiʻi and Upolu. Apia is the capital, on Upolu’s north coast. The
country is independent and distinct from American Samoa, which lies to the east and has a
different political status.
Official name Independent State of Samoa
Capital Apia
Population 205,557 — Samoa official census, November 2021; not a 2025 estimate.
Area 2,831 km²
Languages Samoan and English
Currency Samoan tālā
Government Parliamentary republic with a head of state chosen under constitutional
arrangements
Directory level 11 traditional political districts
THE FLAG
Five white stars form the Southern Cross on a blue panel. Red, white and
blue are associated with courage, purity and freedom in explanations of
the national design.

Getting to know New Zealand
New Zealand sits across the Tasman Sea from Australia. It is often called Aotearoa. Its two
main islands carry very different landscapes, while smaller and distant islands widen the
map. Wellington is the capital; Auckland is the largest city.
Official name New Zealand / Aotearoa
Capital Wellington
Population 5,252,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 263,310 km²
Languages English, Māori and New Zealand Sign Language are official; English received

Currency New Zealand dollar
Government Parliamentary constitutional monarchy

VANUATU / IDENTITY
Getting to know Vanuatu
Vanuatu is a chain of islands between Fiji and Australia. Port Vila is the capital, on Efate.
Luganville on Espiritu Santo is another important town. Many communities speak a local
language as well as Bislama.
Official name Republic of Vanuatu
Capital Port Vila
Population 335,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.
Area 12,189 km²

Currency Vanuatu vatu
Government Parliamentary republic

THE FLAG

and peace.

[4] PACIFIC TERRITORIES / DIRECTORY
France, the United Kingdom and Australia
NEW CALEDONIA
A territory with a special French constitutional arrangement; Nouméa is the main centre.
Grande Terre, the Loyalty Islands and other islands have distinct communities. Kanak
identity, inequality and the future political status remain central issues.
FRENCH POLYNESIA
A French overseas collectivity, with Papeete on Tahiti as the main centre. The Society,
Tuamotu, Marquesas, Austral and Gambier groups stretch across a huge sea area. Local
self-government is not the same as independent statehood.
WALLIS AND FUTUNA
French overseas collectivity with customary kingdoms alongside elected and French
institutions. Mata-Utu is the main administrative centre on Wallis. Futuna and Alofi form
another island group.
PITCAIRN ISLANDS
British Overseas Territory with Adamstown on inhabited Pitcairn. Henderson, Ducie and
Oeno are also included. Isolation makes transport and public services unusually difficult.
NORFOLK ISLAND
Australian external territory between New Zealand and New Caledonia. Kingston is a
historic and administrative setting. Local governance and service arrangements differ
from the mainland states.
OTHER AUSTRALIAN TERRITORIES
Christmas Island and the Cocos (Keeling) Islands lie in the Indian Ocean and are not
treated here as Pacific island countries. Coral Sea, Heard and McDonald, and other
territories have their own status and environments.

Getting to know Palau
Palau is a western Pacific republic with a large main island, smaller inhabited islands and
famous limestone Rock Islands. Ngerulmud is the capital. Koror remains the main urban
and commercial centre, so a map needs to show both.
Official name Republic of Palau
Capital Ngerulmud, in Melekeok state
Population 18,000 — UN mid-2025 estimate, rounded to the nearest thousand.

Languages Palauan and English nationally; some states recognise additional local

light blue field is linked to the nation’s independence and its surrounding
environment.

[7] PACIFIC TERRITORIES / DIRECTORY
United States and New Zealand
GUAM
U.S. territory; main government centre Hagåtña. The island is home to Chamorro heritage
and major military installations. It is different from an independent compact state.
NORTHERN MARIANA ISLANDS
A commonwealth in political union with the United States; Saipan is the main government
centre. The islands include Saipan, Tinian, Rota and northern volcanic islands.
AMERICAN SAMOA
U.S. territory centred on Tutuila and the Pago Pago harbour area, with government
institutions at Fagatogo and Utulei. The Manuʻa group and other islands broaden the map.
It is separate from independent Samoa.
TOKELAU
New Zealand territory consisting of Atafu, Nukunonu and Fakaofo. Decisions involve
island institutions and a national General Fono. There is no single conventional capital
city.
HAWAIʻI
A U.S. state, not a dependent territory or separate country. Honolulu is the capital.
Hawaiian language and culture, the overthrow of the kingdom and annexation belong
within its history.
U.S. MINOR OUTLYING ISLANDS
Baker, Howland, Jarvis, Johnston, Kingman Reef, Midway, Palmyra and Wake have
different administrative and environmental roles. They are not added as independent
countries.

Nauru is a single small island close to the equator. It has no formally designated capital;

places Nauru just to the south. Its twelve points refer to the island’s
original tribes, not its fourteen districts.

Q091: Which overlap between the Asia and Europe volumes explains why their chapter totals cannot be added to count unique countries?

Reference answer: Transcontinental countries can appear in both volumes, so summing chapter totals double-counts countries.

Asia.pdf · location 2
ASIA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
The UN’s Asian geographic grouping includes 48 countries when Hong Kong and Macao
are covered within China. Russia is added because most of its territory lies in Asia. This
gives 49 country chapters. Taiwan receives a separate full profile with its self-government
and disputed international status explained. Transcontinental countries appear in more
than one continental volume where useful.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Singapore uses planning regions; the Philippines uses administrative regions
above the province level. The Maldives uses a geographic atoll directory after its 2026
local-government changes. The level is stated in every chapter. These are not directories
of every municipality or village.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Country population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand.
Taiwan uses its official household-registration count at 31 December 2025. China’s UN
figure is the mainland series; Hong Kong and Macao have separate statistical series. They
are dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the
tables; where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older
internal borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current
affairs were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES
Europe.pdf · location 2
EUROPE / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
Europe has more than one edge
A continent is a useful place to begin. It is not a single culture, a single
political organisation or an agreed list of borders.
What is included
The 44 sovereign countries in the UN’s European geographic grouping form the core.
Türkiye, Cyprus, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan are also included because of
their transcontinental geography or wider European connections. This makes 50 country
chapters. Kosovo receives a separate profile, with its disputed recognition explained.
What the maps do
World locators show position. Regional views name land neighbours. City maps locate
selected centres. Administrative maps and tables name the subdivisions at the level
explained in each chapter. A geographic region is not always an elected province. Distant
islands use separate insets.
What the dates mean
Most population figures are mid-2025 UN estimates, rounded to the nearest thousand.
France uses INSEE’s 1 January 2026 estimate. Vatican City uses its 31 December 2024
resident count. Kosovo uses its 2024 census results, including estimates for northern
municipalities. Government descriptions have a reference date of 11 October 2026.
Borders and disputed control
Ukraine is shown within its internationally recognised borders. Other chapters explain
disputed recognition and areas outside central government control. The maps are
geographic references, not military control maps. India’s official Survey of India outline is
used in every world locator and reproduced in the appendix.
Scope reference: UN M49 geographic grouping. Each country ends with sources and photograph credits. No printed
index is included; PDF bookmarks open the chapters.
WORLD AT A GLANCE / EUROPE F.1

The overlap between Asia and Europe volumes occurs because some countries are transcontinental, meaning they span both continents. Specifically, the UN's geographic grouping includes countries like Russia, Türkiye, Cyprus, Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Kazakhstan in both Asia and Europe. This overlap explains why the chapter totals (49 for Asia and 50 for Europe) cannot be simply added to count unique countries, as these transcontinental countries are counted in both volumes. Q092: How do the Africa and North America volumes distinguish sovereign countries from disputed or non-sovereign places?

Reference answer: Africa has 54 country chapters and a separate disputed Western Sahara section; North America has 23 sovereign chapters and separate non-sovereign places such as Greenland and Puerto Rico.

Africa.pdf · location 2
AFRICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent with many stories
A book can give you a starting point. Each country deserves to be understood on its own
terms.
WHAT IS INCLUDED
All 54 widely recognised sovereign countries in Africa receive complete chapters. Western
Sahara has a separate section because its sovereignty is disputed. The African Union’s
membership count differs: it includes the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Other
territories and disputed places appear in the closing notes.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Uganda and Botswana use broad geographic regions; Libya uses a clearly dated
historical district framework. These are not complete directories of current local councils.
DATES AND BOUNDARIES
Population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. They are
dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the tables;
where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older internal
borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current affairs
were checked for this October 2026 edition.
INDIA AND DISPUTED PLACES
Every world locator uses the official Survey of India international outline. The appendix
repeats it at a larger scale. Other disputed borders and territorial claims are explained
where relevant; map colour alone should not be read as a legal ruling.
FINDING YOUR WAY
Country pages use chapter numbers: 1.1, 1.2 and so on. PDF bookmarks jump directly to
chapters and major sections.

[3] NORTH AMERICA / ABOUT THIS VOLUME
A continent in many voices
North America reaches from Arctic communities to the tropical
isthmus and the islands of the Caribbean.
This book uses a broad geographic definition of North America: Canada and the United States,
Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean. It gives each of the region’s 23 sovereign countries
its own chapter. Greenland, Puerto Rico and other non-sovereign places appear in a separate
reference section.
Start with a place
A country opener gives a photograph, then a flag, population figure and identity panel. Maps
locate neighbours, major towns, administrative divisions and selected physical features. The
following pages explain history, government, livelihoods and culture.
Names should be usable
Crowded division maps use numbers tied to a full-name key. Capitals and local centres appear
in tables. An island, a province and a country are different things; the text makes those
distinctions wherever they matter.
Numbers have dates
Population estimates describe a particular year. They may differ from a national census,
especially where migration is rapid or counting is difficult. The source and year accompany each
figure. Political descriptions use a reference date of 11 October 2026.
India’s outline throughout
Every world locator in this edition uses official Survey of India international-boundary data. The
world-reference appendix uses the same outline. This depicts India’s official territorial position;
it does not settle international boundary disputes.
Reading a country fairly
A chapter can introduce a country without speaking for every resident. Indigenous and
Afro-descendant histories, migration and regional differences belong beside national events.

[7] APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES
Places that need an extra note
RÉUNION AND MAYOTTE
Réunion and Mayotte are French overseas departments in the Indian Ocean. Mayotte
belongs geographically to the Comoros archipelago; Comoros claims it, while France
administers it. Neither is one of the 54 sovereign country chapters.
CEUTA, MELILLA AND THE CANARY ISLANDS
Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish autonomous cities on the North African coast, claimed by
Morocco. Spain’s Canary Islands lie in the Atlantic off northwest Africa. They have no
separate sovereign-country chapter.
SAINT HELENA, ASCENSION AND TRISTAN DA CUNHA
These widely separated Atlantic islands form one British Overseas Territory. Separate
insets are necessary to show their distances. Their connection to Africa is geographic, not
membership among African sovereign states.
CHAGOS AND TROMELIN
Mauritius claims the Chagos Archipelago and Tromelin. The UK and Mauritius signed a
Chagos agreement in 2025, with implementation contested in 2026. France administers
Tromelin. Maps should distinguish claims, treaties and completed transfers.
SOMALILAND
Somaliland has separate institutions and declared independence in 1991. Israel
recognised it in December 2025; Somalia and the African Union reject its separation. The
Somalia chapter uses the prevailing international country outline and explains the limited
recognition.
ABYEI AND OTHER CONTESTED BOUNDARIES
Abyei’s final status remains disputed between Sudan and South Sudan. The Egypt–Sudan
boundary dispute includes Halaib; Kenya–South Sudan claims overlap in the Ilemi
Triangle. Lake Malawi/Nyasa has a Tanzania–Malawi boundary dispute. Regional locators
do not replace legal or diplomatic boundary documentation.

APPENDIX B / TERRITORIES
Places that need an extra note
RÉUNION AND MAYOTTE
Réunion and Mayotte are French overseas departments in the Indian Ocean. Mayotte
belongs geographically to the Comoros archipelago; Comoros claims it, while France
administers it. Neither is one of the 54 sovereign country chapters.
CEUTA, MELILLA AND THE CANARY ISLANDS
Ceuta and Melilla are Spanish autonomous cities on the North African coast, claimed by
Morocco. Spain’s Canary Islands lie in the Atlantic off northwest Africa. They have no
separate sovereign-country chapter.
SAINT HELENA, ASCENSION AND TRISTAN DA CUNHA
These widely separated Atlantic islands form one British Overseas Territory. Separate
insets are necessary to show their distances. Their connection to Africa is geographic, not
membership among African sovereign states.
CHAGOS AND TROMELIN
Mauritius claims the Chagos Archipelago and Tromelin. The UK and Mauritius signed a
Chagos agreement in 2025, with implementation contested in 2026. France administers
Tromelin. Maps should distinguish claims, treaties and completed transfers.
SOMALILAND
Somaliland has separate institutions and declared independence in 1991. Israel
recognised it in December 2025; Somalia and the African Union reject its separation. The
Somalia chapter uses the prevailing international country outline and explains the limited
recognition.
ABYEI AND OTHER CONTESTED BOUNDARIES
Abyei’s final status remains disputed between Sudan and South Sudan. The Egypt–Sudan
boundary dispute includes Halaib; Kenya–South Sudan claims overlap in the Ilemi
Triangle. Lake Malawi/Nyasa has a Tanzania–Malawi boundary dispute. Regional locators
do not replace legal or diplomatic boundary documentation.

territories and disputed places appear in the closing notes.
HOW TO READ THE MAPS
World locators show position; regional maps name land neighbours; city maps locate
selected centres. Physical maps label major landforms, waters and islands. Division maps
connect numbered locations to tables of names and seats. The chosen level is stated
explicitly. Uganda and Botswana use broad geographic regions; Libya uses a clearly dated
historical district framework. These are not complete directories of current local councils.

Population figures are UN mid-2025 estimates rounded to the nearest thousand. They are
dated estimates, not live counts. Recent administrative reforms are included in the tables;
where reliable new boundary shapes are unavailable, locator points replace older internal
borders. Numbered points may locate a division rather than its capital. Current affairs
were checked for this October 2026 edition.

where relevant; map colour alone should not be read as a legal ruling.

# FreeEdit — Product Improvements & Engineering Roadmap

> **Goal:** Turn FreeEdit into a dependable, frictionless way to clean up a recording and export a shareable result — without becoming a bloated video editor.

**Repository:** https://github.com/srbmaury/FreeEdit 
**Document type:** Product and technical improvement proposal 
**Guiding principle:** **Upload → make a few useful edits → preview → export.**

---

## 1. Product Direction

FreeEdit already targets a clear user problem: quick audio/video cleanup. The existing project, as previously reviewed, includes noise reduction using DeepFilterNet3, video trimming, text overlays, blurring/pixelation, previews, and export via a FastAPI/FFmpeg-based processing pipeline.

**Keep the product focused:** A user with a noisy screen recording should be able to make it watchable and shareable in one session. Avoid accounts, social features, collaboration systems, and general-purpose timeline editing in the first release.

### Primary user journey

1. **Drop** a recorded video or audio file into FreeEdit.
2. **Choose** a quick cleanup action (noise removal, trim, silence cleanup, or privacy masking).
3. **Review** a fast preview and adjust the results if needed.
4. **Export** the finished media with an appropriate size/quality preset.
5. **Leave** with the processed file; account creation should not be required.

**North-star metric:** Percentage of successful uploads that produce an exported file. 
**Secondary metrics:** Median time-to-export; processing failure rate; failed export rate; repeat-use rate (if measured in a privacy-preserving way).

---

## 2. Features to Add (Prioritized)

### P0 — One-click silence removal

**Problem:** Tutorial, lecture, and screen recordings commonly contain awkward pauses.

# Seven Practical Open-Source Project Ideas

> **Theme:** One recognizable problem. One complete user journey. One useful output. 
> **Constraints:** No forced sign-up, no AI wrapper, no social graph, no marketplace needed to deliver first-session value.

These are product concepts, **not claims that no competing products exist**. Each idea should be validated against available tools and with a handful of actual users before building extensively.

---

## Quick Comparison

| # | Project | User's job-to-be-done | Difficulty | Strongest differentiator to explore |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | GhostLayer | Remove unintended information from files | Medium | Inspect → explain → clean → verify |
| 02 | DiffPaper | Understand what changed between two PDFs | High | Layout-aware comparison and readable report |
| 03 | TableLift | Export messy webpage tables cleanly | Medium | Visual selection and reliable normalization |
| 04 | ProofPack | Capture an actionable bug report | High | Replay context with privacy controls |
| 05 | NearDrop | Transfer files directly between devices | High | Smooth cross-platform pairing/resume |
| 06 | SubShift | Fix subtitle timing | Low–Medium | Simple visual drift correction |
| 07 | FormForge | Fill non-interactive PDFs | Medium | Precise WYSIWYG placement and export |

---

## 01 — GhostLayer

**Tagline:** Know what a file reveals before you share it.

### Problem

Images can contain camera/GPS metadata. Documents can contain authorship, comments, tracked revisions, attachments, or other nonobvious information. Users rarely inspect these before sharing.

### Single user journey

`Drop file → Inspect metadata/hidden content → Select safe removals → Verify preview → Download cleaned copy`

### MVP

## 1. Product Direction

FreeEdit already targets a clear user problem: quick audio/video cleanup. The existing project, as previously reviewed, includes noise reduction using DeepFilterNet3, video trimming, text overlays, blurring/pixelation, previews, and export via a FastAPI/FFmpeg-based processing pipeline.

**Keep the product focused:** A user with a noisy screen recording should be able to make it watchable and shareable in one session. Avoid accounts, social features, collaboration systems, and general-purpose timeline editing in the first release.

### Primary user journey

1. **Drop** a recorded video or audio file into FreeEdit.
2. **Choose** a quick cleanup action (noise removal, trim, silence cleanup, or privacy masking).
3. **Review** a fast preview and adjust the results if needed.
4. **Export** the finished media with an appropriate size/quality preset.
5. **Leave** with the processed file; account creation should not be required.

**North-star metric:** Percentage of successful uploads that produce an exported file.

## 2. Features to Add (Prioritized)

## 6. Definition of Success

A first-time user can upload a typical screen recording, remove background noise, shorten pauses, hide one on-screen detail, preview the result, and export a playable file **without help or an account**.

> **FreeEdit should feel like a utility, not a video-production platform.**

> **Constraints:** No forced sign-up, no AI wrapper, no social graph, no marketplace needed to deliver first-session value.

These are product concepts, **not claims that no competing products exist**. Each idea should be validated against available tools and with a handful of actual users before building extensively.
